title: CXO Leadership Styles
tagline: Lead from the top table: the styles, roles, decisions, governance and presence that separate a C-suite leader from a senior manager, anywhere in the world.
sectors: Listed companies, multinationals and family-owned groups
Banks, development finance and financial services
description:
Getting to the C-suite rewards functional excellence. Succeeding there demands something else: leading leaders instead of doing the work, owning the whole enterprise instead of one function, making big bets with half the facts, and answering to a board, investors, regulators and the public at the same time.

This certification is built for senior managers and executives on that path, wherever they work. You will learn the main **leadership style models** and when each one helps or hurts at the top, what a **CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CIO and CMO** each really owe the business, and how to turn a group of strong functional heads into a real **executive team**.

You will practise **strategic decisions under uncertainty** with scenarios, pre-mortems and the reversible versus irreversible test; work through **boards and corporate governance** using the G20/OECD Principles and examples from the UK, US, India, Pakistan and beyond; and lead through **culture change, transformation and crisis**. The course closes with **executive presence, ethical tone at the top and succession**, including your own.

Every stage uses **real cases** from Ford, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Shell, Wells Fargo, Satyam, Johnson & Johnson and Uber. Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built on realistic boardroom scenarios from around the world.
audience: Senior managers and heads of function preparing for a first C-suite or executive committee role
Newly appointed CXOs who want a structured view of how the top job differs from the one below it
Leaders in family-owned and sponsor-led groups moving to professional, board-governed management
High-potential leaders in multinational and regional groups named in succession plans for CXO roles
Company secretaries, strategy and HR leaders who work closely with boards and executive teams
outcomes: Choose and flex leadership styles deliberately, using the six emotional-intelligence styles, situational leadership, transformational and servant models
Explain the distinct mandate and mindset of each C-suite role and build an executive team that acts as one first team
Make and frame strategic decisions under uncertainty with scenarios, pre-mortems, expected value and the reversible versus irreversible test
Work effectively with a board under international governance principles and national codes, including related-party and conflict situations
Shape culture and lead transformation and crisis, communicating clearly with staff, investors, regulators and the public
Set an ethical tone at the top, build executive presence and own succession, including your own development

quest.name: The Succession Year
quest.premise: Tessaly Foods, a listed dairy and juice group headquartered in Dubai, with plants in Kenya, Pakistan, Malaysia and Brazil and controlled by the Vos family, has announced that its long-serving CEO Rafael Montoya will retire in twelve months. The board has named two internal candidates: COO Kwame Asante and you, the new Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer. Independent director Mei Lin Tan becomes your mentor. Over five stages you will lead an executive team, make a USD 720 million bet, face the board and a crisis, and sit the succession interview.

badge.name: Top Table Leader
badge.description: Awarded to leaders who can flex their style, lead an executive team, decide under uncertainty, work with a board and set the tone at the top.

cast.name: Kwame Asante
cast.role: Chief Operating Officer, the other candidate

sessions.title: Leadership Styles at the Top Table
sessions.summary: The move into the C-suite changes what leadership means. Learn the main style models (the six emotional-intelligence styles, situational leadership, transformational versus transactional, servant leadership) and how to flex them when you lead leaders, not tasks.
objectives: Explain how the job changes when a functional head becomes an enterprise leader
Describe the six emotional-intelligence leadership styles and when each helps or harms
Apply situational leadership by matching your style to a leader's competence and commitment
Distinguish transformational, transactional and servant leadership and how they combine

cards.title: The announcement
cards.setting: Thirtieth floor, Tessaly Foods head office, Dubai. Monday, 8:40 am.

lines.text: The executive floor is unusually quiet. A message from the company secretary has asked every ExCo member to be in the boardroom by 8:45.
Nineteen years. I took this company from one milk plant outside Nairobi to a USD 1.4 billion group selling in eleven countries. In twelve months, I retire.
The board has asked for two internal candidates. Kwame, our COO. And our new Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer. You.
Congratulations. And good luck. You'll need it on this floor. We do things fast here, and we do them Rafael's way.
That afternoon, independent director Mei Lin Tan, just in from Singapore, invites you for coffee in the board lounge.
I chair the board's HR and remuneration committee, and I will be your mentor this year. First lesson: the board is not judging how good you are at strategy.
Engagement on this floor fell eleven points last year. Rafael built this company by command. The next CEO has to lead leaders, across four continents. So, how do you lead?

cards.title: From function head to enterprise leader

scenes.heading: What got you here
scenes.narration: You reached the top table by being the best at something: finance, sales, plants, technology. That expertise is now the price of entry, not the job.

scenes.heading: The whole enterprise
scenes.narration: A C-suite leader owns outcomes for the whole company. Your function's wins mean little if the enterprise loses. You trade some of your team's interests for the company's.

scenes.heading: Your first team
scenes.narration: Your first team is now your peers at the executive table, not the function that reports to you. You lead your function on behalf of that team.

scenes.heading: Leading through leaders
scenes.narration: Almost nobody you affect reports to you directly. You work through other senior leaders, so how you lead them is multiplied hundreds of times down the organisation.

scenes.heading: Your shadow
scenes.narration: People copy what you do, not what you say. Your moods, your questions and the behaviour you tolerate cast a long shadow. At the top, there is no such thing as a private bad day.

scenes.heading: A repertoire, not a habit
scenes.narration: So the question is not which style you have. It is which style this moment needs, and whether you can switch to it on purpose.

cards.title: The shift in the job
cards.caption: Most new CXOs struggle not for lack of skill but because they keep doing the job below.

items.label: Focus
items.right: Win for the whole company, even at my function's cost

items.label: First team
items.left: The people who report to me
items.right: My peers at the executive table

items.label: Value added
items.right: Direction, capital allocation, talent and culture

items.label: Time horizon
items.right: Three to ten years, while still delivering this year

items.label: Influence
items.right: Through leaders, the board and external stakeholders

cards.title: Six styles leaders draw on
cards.body:
Research on emotional intelligence describes **six leadership styles**. The strongest leaders use several and switch deliberately.

| Style | In one line | Best used when |
|---|---|---|
| **Visionary** | "Come with me" towards a clear picture | Change needs a new direction |
| **Coaching** | "Try this" to grow the person | Someone wants to develop |
| **Affiliative** | "People come first" | Trust is broken, wounds need healing |
| **Democratic** | "What do you think?" | You need buy-in or fresh ideas, and have time |
| **Pacesetting** | "Do as I do, now" | A skilled, motivated team needs fast results |
| **Commanding** | "Do what I say" | A genuine crisis or turnaround |

The first four tend to **lift the climate**. Pacesetting and commanding get quick results but **damage climate when overused**. The trap at the top: these two feel efficient, so they become habits.

cards.title: Hear the style
cards.prompt: Each line was overheard on Tessaly's executive floor. Match it to the style it signals.

pairs.right: "In five years we are the brand every family in our markets trusts for safe milk. Here is why, and here is your part in it."
"You want to run a region one day. Let's use this distributor dispute to stretch you. What options do you see?"
"Before we talk targets, how is the team holding up after the layoffs? Let's spend today on that."
"I don't have the answer on the new pricing tier. I want each of you to argue a case before we decide."
"I redid your deck over the weekend. This is the standard. Match it by Thursday."
"The plant is on fire. Evacuate now, everyone to the assembly point, no questions until headcount is done."

cards.question: Rafael has run ExCo by command for years. Things are not in crisis, but morale has fallen and ideas have dried up. Which change of style would most likely lift the executive climate?
options: Shift towards visionary and democratic styles: set a clear direction and genuinely invite views on how to get there
Shift to pacesetting: show the team the standard by doing more of the work himself
Keep commanding, but explain the reasons for each order more politely
cards.explanation: Without a real crisis, constant commanding drains initiative. Visionary and democratic styles tend to rebuild climate: people know where the company is going and have a voice in how. Pacesetting, the other climate-damaging style, would make things worse.

cards.title: Situational leadership: four ways to lead one person
cards.caption: Match how much you direct and how much you support to the person's competence and commitment on this specific task.

items.label: Directing
items.detail: High direction, low support. For someone new to the task but keen: clear goals, steps and close follow-up.

items.label: Coaching
items.detail: High direction, high support. Some skill, confidence dipping: still guide, but explain, listen and encourage.

items.label: Delegating
items.detail: Low direction, low support. Skilled and committed: agree the outcome, hand over the decisions, stay available.

items.label: Supporting
items.detail: Low direction, high support. Capable but unsure or demotivated: involve them, listen, build confidence.

cards.front: What two things do you assess before choosing a style?
cards.back: Competence (knowledge and skill for this task) and commitment (confidence and motivation for it). The same person can need different styles on different tasks.

cards.front: A brilliant new CIO, enthusiastic but new to dairy supply chains. Which style for the plant-systems project?
cards.back: Directing on that task: clear goals, context and frequent check-ins, because competence in this domain is still low while commitment is high.

cards.front: Your seasoned Head of Treasury has done this refinancing five times and loves it.
cards.back: Delegating: agree the outcome and limits, then step back. Close supervision here would insult and demotivate.

cards.front: What goes wrong if you over-supervise a capable executive?
cards.back: You waste your time, signal distrust and slowly push a strong leader into passivity or out of the company.

cards.front: What goes wrong if you delegate too early?
cards.back: That is abdication, not delegation. The person fails without support, and both of you lose confidence.

cards.title: The 360 nobody wanted to read
cards.setting: Board lounge, two weeks later. Mei Lin slides a printed 360-degree feedback report across the table.

lines.text: Your team rates your strategic thinking very highly. Then this: 'Rewrites our work at midnight.' 'Sets a pace nobody can keep.' 'Hard to bring bad news to.'
You recognise every line. You were a star strategy partner at a consulting firm. Doing it better yourself always worked.
That is pacesetting. It works for a short sprint with a skilled team. Run it for months and good people either burn out or stop trying.
(passing in the corridor) Don't feel bad. Mine says I'm 'Rafael junior'. Apparently commanding is genetic on this floor.
Notice what both of you do: you treat leaders as executors. The board wants someone who makes other leaders bigger. Let's look at how.

cards.title: The full range of leadership
cards.caption: Transformational leadership builds on top of solid transactional foundations; it does not replace them. Doing nothing sits at the bottom.

items.label: Transformational
items.detail: Lifts people beyond self-interest via four I's: idealised influence (role-model), inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration.

items.label: Contingent reward
items.detail: Transactional: clear agreements on what will be delivered and what people get in return.

items.label: Management by exception
items.detail: Transactional: step in when standards are missed, actively by monitoring or passively once problems surface.

items.label: Laissez-faire
items.detail: Absent leadership: avoiding decisions and involvement. Consistently the least effective.

cards.title: Transformational or transactional?
cards.prompt: Sort each behaviour by Tessaly executives into the leadership approach it shows.

items.text: Linking the cold-chain project to the purpose of 'safe milk for every child'
Agreeing a bonus pool tied to hitting the quarterly EBITDA target
Asking the ExCo to challenge the assumption that online grocery will stay small in our African markets
Reviewing the variance report and stepping in only where plants miss their cost targets
Spending time with each direct report on their own career aspirations and strengths
Following up when a KPI turns red and agreeing corrective action
Visibly cutting her own perks first when cost cuts are announced
Promising the sales head a promotion if the Kenya launch hits plan

cards.question: Which of these is an example of intellectual stimulation, one of the four elements of transformational leadership?
options: Telling the team that the CEO personally values each of them
Inviting the team to question long-held assumptions and try new approaches to old problems
Paying an on-the-spot cash award for meeting a deadline
Setting out a compelling picture of where the company will be in five years
cards.explanation: Intellectual stimulation means encouraging people to challenge assumptions and think in new ways. A five-year picture is inspirational motivation, personal attention is individualised consideration, and a cash award for a deadline is transactional contingent reward.

cards.title: Servant leadership and the humble-but-fierce leader
cards.body:
**Servant leadership** flips the pyramid: the leader's first question is *what do my people need to grow and succeed?* Its hallmarks are listening, empathy, stewardship of the organisation and commitment to people's growth.

- It is **not** softness. A servant leader still sets high standards and makes hard calls; the difference is **whose interests the leader is serving** when doing so.
- Its risks at the top: slow decisions if everything becomes consultation, and being exploited by self-serving colleagues.

Studies of companies that moved from good to great performance found leaders who combined **personal humility** (credit to others, modest about themselves, ambition for the company not for self) with **intense professional will** (relentless about results, willing to take tough decisions).

The lesson for CXOs: charisma is optional. Humility plus resolve is not.

cards.title: Real case: Microsoft's 'learn-it-all' reset (2014 on)
cards.body:
Satya Nadella became Microsoft's third CEO in February 2014. The company was rich but widely seen as having missed the shift to mobile, with internal rivalries slowing it down.

Nadella made **culture** a personal CEO priority. Drawing on psychologist Carol Dweck's research on the **growth mindset**, he asked Microsoft to move from a culture of 'know-it-alls' to one of '**learn-it-alls**'.

- **Visionary:** a clear bet on cloud computing and a new mission statement.
- **Coaching and humility:** he talked openly about learning, listening and empathy, and worked with former rivals, for example releasing Office for the iPad in 2014.
- **Resolve:** he made hard calls, including large write-downs and job cuts in the phone business.

By 2021 Microsoft's market value had passed USD 2 trillion. Nadella described the journey in his 2017 book *Hit Refresh*.

**The lesson:** humility and resolve can sit in one leader, and culture change starts with the CEO's own behaviour.

cards.title: The passed-over plant head
cards.situation: Rafiq Soomro has run Tessaly's Karachi milk plant for 18 years. He knows every machine and every union leader, and the plant's results are the best in the group. He applied for the new Group Head of Manufacturing role but it went to an outsider. Since then he has gone quiet in meetings, missed two improvement deadlines and told colleagues he 'just runs the machines now'. He reports into your transformation programme for the plant automation project. How do you lead him?

choices.text: Spell out the project plan in detail, set weekly milestones and review his progress closely.
choices.outcome: Rafiq hears it as 'we don't trust you either'. His competence was never the problem, so heavy direction feels like a demotion on top of a disappointment. He complies to the letter and contributes nothing extra.

choices.text: Meet him one to one, acknowledge the disappointment, ask for his view of how automation should work in Karachi and involve him in key decisions.
choices.outcome: This is a supporting style: low direction, high support, because his skill is high but his commitment has dipped. Rafiq's ideas reshape the rollout, and two months later he is presenting the plan to ExCo himself.

choices.text: Leave him alone with the full project; he is the most capable person for it and will come round.
choices.outcome: Delegating fits someone both skilled and committed. Rafiq is skilled but disengaged, so leaving him alone reads as indifference. The project drifts and you discover the slippage late.

choices.text: Tell him that the decision is final and that the company expects him to be professional about it.
choices.outcome: True, but it addresses none of what is actually driving his behaviour. A commanding message to a hurt, capable veteran usually deepens the withdrawal or prompts an exit.

cards.title: Choosing your style on purpose
cards.prompt: Mei Lin's routine for walking into any leadership moment. Put the steps in order.
steps: Read the situation: how urgent is it, and what is at stake?
Read the people: their competence and commitment for this task
Choose the style the moment needs, not the one you find most comfortable
Say how you are going to run it, e.g. 'I will decide this one' or 'I want your views first'
Watch the effect on energy, ideas and results
Shift style as the situation or the people change

cards.title: The pacesetter's trap
cards.body:
Most new CXOs were promoted for personal excellence, so pacesetting is their default under pressure.

- **Signs you are in it:** you redo work, you are the bottleneck for approvals, people bring you finished answers but never problems.
- **Why it bites at the top:** your team are themselves senior leaders. Redoing their work tells their teams that their boss is not trusted.
- **What to do:** agree the standard and the outcome up front, then coach to the gap instead of closing it yourself. Ask "what would you do?" before you say what you would do.

cards.title: Real case: Ford's red slide (2006–2009)
cards.body:
When Alan Mulally became Ford's CEO in 2006, the company was on its way to a loss of more than USD 12 billion that year. He borrowed over USD 20 billion, pledging most of Ford's assets, and set one direction: **One Ford**.

His key tool was a weekly **Business Plan Review**. Every executive showed their projects in green, yellow or red. For weeks every chart was green, while the company lost billions.

Then Mark Fields, head of the Americas, showed a **red** slide: a launch was on hold over a technical fault. The room expected him to be punished. Mulally **applauded**, and asked who could help. Within weeks the charts turned honest and problems were fixed faster.

In 2009 Ford was the only one of the big three US carmakers that avoided both bankruptcy and a government bailout.

**The lesson:** a visionary direction, transactional discipline (weekly facts) and a leader who makes bad news safe, all working together.

cards.question: Layla, the CFO, has led budget cycles for years and is excited about leading Tessaly's first sustainability-linked loan, a product she has never handled. Under situational leadership, how should you lead her on this specific task at first?
options: Delegating, because she is a senior and committed leader
Directing, with clear goals, context and close early check-ins, because her skill on this task is new while her commitment is high
Supporting, because senior leaders mainly need encouragement
Commanding, because a loan has financial risk
cards.explanation: Situational leadership is assessed task by task. On a new product, Layla's competence is still low while her commitment is high, which calls for more direction early on. Delegating would fit her normal budgeting work, not this new task.

cards.title: Thirtieth floor cleared
items: At the top your first team is your peers at the executive table, and your value comes from direction, capital, talent and culture, not expert answers.
The six emotional-intelligence styles: visionary, coaching, affiliative and democratic tend to build climate; pacesetting and commanding damage it when overused.
Situational leadership matches direction and support to each person's competence and commitment for a specific task.
Transformational leadership (role-model, purpose, challenge, individual attention) builds on transactional foundations of clear deals and follow-up.
Servant leadership and humble-but-determined leaders show that serving people's growth and demanding high standards go together.
Choose your style on purpose, say which one you are using, and watch the effect.

cards.prompt: Think about the last month. Which of the six styles did you use most, and which did you never use? Name one leader in your team who needs a different style from you than the one you usually give them, and what you will do differently next week.

quiz.question: A newly appointed CMO keeps arguing in ExCo for her marketing budget even when the company has agreed to shift money to plant safety. In enterprise-leadership terms, what is she missing?
options: She is not yet using a coaching style with her marketing team, so they cannot accept the reallocation
She still treats her function, not the executive team, as her first team
She should escalate the budget question to the board
She is being too democratic in a crisis
quiz.explanation: An enterprise leader's first team is the executive team, and she must sometimes accept that her function gives way for the company's sake. Coaching her team or going to the board does not fix the underlying mindset problem.

quiz.question: Which of the six emotional-intelligence styles is defined by the leader setting out a compelling destination and letting people find their own route to it?
options: Democratic
Pacesetting
Affiliative
Visionary
quiz.explanation: The visionary style mobilises people towards a clear picture of the future and leaves freedom in how to get there. Democratic builds the answer together, affiliative focuses on harmony and people, and pacesetting leads by personal example and speed.

quiz.question: A fire at the Jebel Ali warehouse in Dubai means staff must be evacuated and stock moved within hours. Which leadership style is most appropriate in the first hours?
options: Commanding: clear, immediate instructions with no debate until people are safe
Democratic: gather views from the warehouse team before deciding, since they know the site better than anyone
Coaching: use the incident to develop the warehouse manager
Affiliative: focus on how people are feeling about the fire
quiz.explanation: In a genuine emergency, commanding is the right tool: speed and clarity save people and assets. Coaching and democratic styles have their place later, in the recovery and the lessons-learned review.

quiz.question: Why is the pacesetting style risky when it becomes a CXO's everyday habit?
options: Because it relies on long consultation with the team, which slows down decisions that the business needs quickly
Because it is only allowed during a formal crisis
Because it tends to overwhelm people and erodes initiative, even if it gets fast results in the short run
Because it focuses too much on people's feelings instead of results
quiz.explanation: Pacesetting sets very high standards by personal example and works briefly with a skilled, motivated team. Sustained, it overwhelms people and makes them wait for the leader. Slow consultation describes the democratic style's risk, and a focus on feelings describes affiliative.

quiz.question: Your Head of Exports is highly skilled at opening new markets but has lost confidence after a failed launch in Central Asia. Under situational leadership, which style best fits her next market entry?
options: Directing
Supporting
Delegating
Commanding
quiz.explanation: High competence with dipped commitment calls for supporting: low direction, high support, listening and building confidence. Directing would wrongly treat her skill as low; delegating fits someone both skilled and confident. Commanding is not a situational leadership style.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes contingent reward, a core element of transactional leadership?
options: Clear agreement on what the person will deliver and what they will receive in return
Inspiring people to put the company's purpose ahead of their own interests
Stepping in only after a serious problem has already surfaced, then agreeing corrective action with the person
Avoiding decisions and leaving the team to work things out
quiz.explanation: Contingent reward is the transactional deal: delivery in exchange for agreed rewards. Inspiring beyond self-interest is transformational; stepping in after problems surface is passive management by exception; avoiding decisions is laissez-faire.

quiz.question: In the full range of leadership, how does transformational leadership relate to transactional leadership?
options: They are opposites, so a leader must choose one
Transactional leadership is always more effective in hierarchical cultures, where clear rewards are expected
Transformational leadership is only for CEOs, transactional for everyone else
Transformational leadership builds on a solid transactional base of clear agreements and follow-up
quiz.explanation: Effective leaders use both: clear deals and follow-up keep the basics working, and transformational behaviours lift effort and commitment above that. They are complements, not alternatives, and neither is reserved for a single level or country.

quiz.question: A colleague says servant leadership means 'never upsetting your team and letting them decide everything'. What is the best correction?
options: That is correct; servant leaders avoid hard calls
Servant leadership only applies in NGOs and public sector bodies
Servant leaders put people's growth first but still set high standards and make hard decisions
Servant leadership means the leader's first duty is to serve the board and shareholders rather than the staff below
quiz.explanation: Servant leadership centres on serving people's growth and the organisation's long-term good, which includes high standards and tough decisions. It is not abdication, it is not limited to non-profits, and it is not about serving the board instead of staff.

quiz.question: A high-potential regional sales manager tells you she wants to be ready for a director role in two years and asks for stretch work. Which style should you lead with in your conversations with her?
options: Pacesetting, so she sees exactly what top performance looks like by watching you do the hardest work yourself
Affiliative, because her feelings come first
Coaching, linking stretch assignments and feedback to her development goals
Commanding, so she learns discipline
quiz.explanation: The coaching style fits a person who wants to grow: it connects daily work to longer-term development through stretch and feedback. Pacesetting would show the standard but not build her capability; commanding and affiliative do not fit her request.

quiz.question: When is the democratic style likely to backfire for a CEO?
options: During an urgent crisis where a quick, clear decision is needed
When the CEO wants buy-in for a major direction
When the team has more expertise on the question than the CEO and the CEO needs their knowledge
When the CEO is genuinely unsure of the best path
quiz.explanation: Democratic leadership needs time and works when buy-in, expertise or fresh ideas matter. In an urgent crisis, long consultation delays the decisive action needed. The other three situations are exactly where the democratic style helps.

sessions.title: The C-Suite Roles and the Executive Team
sessions.summary: Each C-suite role carries its own mandate and mindset, and a room full of strong function heads is not yet a team. Learn what the CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CIO and CMO each owe the business, and how to build an executive team that debates hard, decides clearly and speaks with one voice.
objectives: Describe the core mandate and mindset of the CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CIO and CMO
Explain the layers of executive team health, from trust to collective results
Use clear decision rights and 'disagree and commit' to end decision churn
Design executive meetings that produce decisions rather than status reports

cards.title: Three weeks in the chair
cards.setting: ExCo meeting room, Tessaly Foods, Dubai. Rafael is on a three-week investor roadshow in Asia and has asked you to chair ExCo in his absence.

lines.text: (voice note from the airport) Three weeks. Keep the ship steady. And get a decision on the new UHT line for the Johor plant. It has been on the agenda since March.
Item one: each executive reads out their function's numbers. Forty minutes pass. Nobody asks a question.
The UHT line is simple. USD 45 million, capacity sold out by year two. Operations needs it now.
With interest rates where they are and the ringgit moving against the dollar, I cannot sign off a payback built on last year's milk prices. Finance says not yet.
Finance always says not yet.
Silence. The CMO studies her phone. The CIO says the item should be 'taken offline'. The meeting ends with no decision, for the sixth time.
(by message from Singapore that evening) The board sees an ExCo of talented individuals and no team. Fix that in three weeks and they will notice.

scenes.heading: The CEO
scenes.narration: The CEO sets direction, decides where capital and talent go, builds the top team, shapes culture and represents the company to the board and the outside world. Few of those tasks can be delegated.

scenes.heading: The CFO
scenes.narration: The CFO guards the numbers and the controls, but the bigger value is as a partner in strategy: testing assumptions, allocating capital and funding the plan sensibly.

scenes.heading: The COO
scenes.narration: The COO turns strategy into daily execution across plants, supply chain and service. The role varies most between companies, and it often complements the CEO's own strengths.

scenes.heading: The CHRO
scenes.narration: The CHRO owns the talent agenda: leadership pipeline, succession, rewards and culture. A strong CHRO advises the board's HR and remuneration committee, not only the CEO.

scenes.heading: The CIO and CMO
scenes.narration: The CIO makes technology, data and cyber security work for the business. The CMO brings the voice of the customer and owns growth from brands and markets. Increasingly, they cannot succeed without each other.

scenes.heading: A system, not a list
scenes.narration: Each role creates healthy tension with the others: growth against prudence, speed against control, today against tomorrow. The CEO's job is to keep that tension productive, not to remove it.

cards.title: Who owns what?
cards.prompt: Match each C-suite role to the mandate that belongs to it most clearly.

pairs.right: Sets overall direction, chooses the top team and is accountable to the board for the whole company
Integrity of financial reporting and controls, plus capital allocation and funding strategy
Reliable day-to-day execution across plants, supply chain and service delivery
Leadership pipeline, succession, reward design and support to the board's HR committee
Technology architecture, data and cyber resilience as enablers of the strategy
Customer insight, brand health and profitable growth from markets and channels

cards.title: Tessaly's ExCo, by the numbers
cards.caption: Your quick audit of the last six months of ExCo meetings, before you chair your first one.

items.label: Time on status updates
items.detail: Functions reading out numbers already in the pre-read.

items.label: Decisions reopened
items.detail: Agreed in the room, then reopened in one-to-ones with the CEO.

items.label: Strategic items deferred
items.detail: The UHT line decision, carried forward since March.

items.label: Cross-functional KPIs
items.detail: Every executive is measured only on their own function.

cards.question: Which of these responsibilities can a CEO least afford to delegate?
options: Preparing the monthly management accounts
Choosing and shaping the executive team and deciding where major capital goes
Negotiating routine supplier contracts
Running the annual employee engagement survey
cards.explanation: Direction, the top team and major capital allocation sit at the heart of the CEO's job and cannot be handed off. The other tasks matter but belong naturally to the CFO, procurement and HR.

cards.front: 'The CFO is the company's scorekeeper.'
cards.back: Only half true. Stewardship of reporting and controls is non-negotiable, but the CFO adds most value as a strategy partner: challenging assumptions and allocating capital.

cards.front: 'The COO is always the CEO-in-waiting.'
cards.back: Not necessarily. Some COOs are successors, some are a permanent execution partner to an outward-facing CEO, and some companies have no COO at all.

cards.front: 'HR is an administrative function.'
cards.back: At C-suite level, the CHRO is the steward of talent and culture and a key adviser on executive succession and pay to the board.

cards.front: 'Cyber security is the CIO's problem.'
cards.back: The CIO leads the defences, but cyber is a business risk that the CEO, ExCo and board own together.

cards.front: 'Marketing spends; finance saves.'
cards.back: Both are investing. Strong CMOs and CFOs agree how to measure the return on brand and market spend together.

cards.title: The CEO–CFO partnership
cards.body:
The most important pairing at the top is usually the CEO and the CFO.

- **Constructive tension:** the CEO pushes for ambition and growth; the CFO tests the assumptions and protects the balance sheet. Both are needed. A CFO who always agrees is a warning sign; one who always blocks is another.
- **One version of the truth:** they agree the numbers before the board sees them, so debates are about choices, not about whose spreadsheet is right.
- **Independence that the board relies on:** the CFO signs off the accounts and is often the board's and audit committee's first line of comfort. A CEO who leans on the CFO to dress up results puts both careers at risk.
- **Shared capital discipline:** clear hurdle rates, post-investment reviews of big projects and honest reforecasts.

At Tessaly, Layla's 'not yet' is not obstruction. It is a missing conversation about assumptions.

cards.title: Real case: Tim Cook, Apple's COO (1998–2011)
cards.body:
Tim Cook joined Apple in 1998 to fix its operations. Steve Jobs was the product visionary and the public face; Cook made the machine run. He closed factories and warehouses, moved manufacturing to contract partners and cut inventory sharply, which freed cash at a time Apple badly needed it.

He became **COO in 2005** and ran the company day to day during Jobs's medical leaves. In **August 2011** he became CEO. In 2018 Apple became the first US listed company valued at USD 1 trillion.

**What it shows about the C-suite:**

- The COO role is often shaped to **complement** the CEO: an outward-facing, product-led CEO paired with an execution-focused COO.
- A COO can be a successor, but that is a board choice, not an automatic promotion.
- A successor who is very different from the founder can still keep the strategy and culture going while running the company in their own style.

cards.title: Five layers of a healthy executive team
cards.caption: Each layer rests on the one below. Without trust at the base, everything above it is fragile.

items.label: Collective results
items.detail: The team measures itself on the company's results, not on functional scorecards or personal status.

items.label: Peer accountability
items.detail: Executives call each other out on commitments and behaviour, instead of leaving it all to the CEO.

items.label: Commitment
items.detail: Clear decisions that everyone supports in public, even those who argued against them.

items.label: Healthy conflict
items.detail: Open, robust debate about ideas and data, focused on the issue rather than the person.

items.label: Trust
items.detail: Leaders are willing to admit mistakes, gaps and doubts to each other without fear.

cards.title: The meeting after the meeting
cards.setting: Corridor outside the ExCo room, five minutes after the meeting.

lines.text: Off the record? Layla's finance team kills every project that isn't theirs. I'll get the UHT line through when Rafael is back. He always signs for me.
Ten minutes later, Layla stops by your office with a printed sensitivity analysis she did not show in the room.
If milk prices rise 15%, the payback goes from four years to seven. I didn't want to embarrass Kwame in front of everyone.
(when you call her) There it is. The real debate happens in corridors and in Rafael's office. In the room, everyone is polite and nothing is decided.
That is artificial harmony sitting on low trust. Your job is to bring the conflict into the room, then make the decision stick.

cards.title: Healthy team or warning sign?
cards.prompt: Sort what you see at different executive tables into healthy team behaviour or a warning sign.

items.text: The CFO challenges the CMO's launch assumptions in the meeting, with data
Decisions are reopened in one-to-ones with the CEO after the meeting
An executive admits in ExCo that her project is three months late and asks for help
Meetings are calm and polite but the same item has been deferred for months
The COO tells a peer directly that her team keeps missing shared deadlines
Each executive cascades a different version of the same decision to their teams
Part of every executive's bonus depends on company-wide results
Executives only speak about their own function's numbers

cards.title: Decision rights for a big call
cards.caption: Before debating a major decision, agree who plays which role. Most decision churn comes from not knowing who actually decides.

items.label: Recommend
items.detail: One owner gathers the facts, frames the options and puts forward a proposal.

items.label: Input
items.detail: Those with relevant knowledge are consulted. Their views are heard, not voted.

items.label: Agree
items.detail: A small number with a formal veto, such as legal or compliance. Keep this list very short.

items.label: Decide
items.detail: One person or body makes the call and is accountable for it.

items.label: Execute
items.detail: Those who carry the decision out, with clear owners and dates.

cards.title: Breaking the UHT deadlock
cards.situation: Week two. The UHT line is back on the agenda. Kwame is adamant, Layla is cautious, and you know both have hidden information. Rafael has delegated the decision to ExCo while he is away, provided Layla as CFO confirms the funding plan. You have 90 minutes. How do you run the item?

choices.text: Postpone again until Rafael returns, so the decision has the CEO's full authority.
choices.outcome: A seventh deferral. Kwame plans to lobby Rafael privately, Layla's analysis never reaches the room, and the board's view of 'no team' is confirmed. You had the authority and did not use it.

choices.text: Ask Kwame to own the recommendation, ask Layla to present her sensitivities in the room, invite open challenge, then decide with ExCo and agree one message that everyone backs.
choices.outcome: Debate gets heated but stays on the data. The team agrees a phased version: commit to the civil works now, order the line once milk-price hedging is in place. Kwame is not fully happy but commits publicly, and so does Layla. Decision recorded, one message cascaded.

choices.text: Put it to a vote and go with the majority.
choices.outcome: You get a decision, but voting turns colleagues into winners and losers and skips the real debate on Layla's numbers. The losing side feels no obligation to commit, and the decision is reopened when Rafael returns.

choices.text: Decide yourself in favour of Kwame, since operations knows capacity best.
choices.outcome: You decide without the CFO's funding confirmation, which was Rafael's condition, and without hearing the risk analysis. Layla escalates to the audit committee chair. Speed without process is not leadership.

cards.question: After a full debate, ExCo decides to phase the UHT line. Kwame argued for building it all at once. What does 'disagree and commit' require of him now?
options: He supports the decision fully in public and with his team, while his disagreement stays on record in ExCo
He can tell his team he opposed it, as long as he does not block it
He should raise it again privately with the CEO
He can delay implementation until conditions prove him right
cards.explanation: Disagree and commit means the debate happens in the room and, once decided, everyone owns the decision as if it were their own. Telling his team he opposed it, lobbying the CEO or slow-walking it all undermine collective responsibility.

cards.title: Real case: Amazon's 'disagree and commit' (2016)
cards.body:
In his 2016 letter to shareholders, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos set out how a large company can keep making decisions quickly. Two ideas from that letter are now widely copied:

- **Decide with less than full information.** He suggested most decisions can be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had; waiting for 90% usually means being slow.
- **Disagree and commit.** If you have conviction on a direction even without consensus, say so, and ask people to commit anyway. Bezos described doing it himself: he disagreed with a team about green-lighting an original series for Amazon Studios, told them so, and committed to backing it fully.

**What it shows:** commitment does not need consensus. It needs a real debate, a clear decision-maker and a decision that everyone, **including the most senior person**, then supports in public. Disagree and commit is not the same as staying silent: the disagreement is voiced first, in the room.

cards.title: Running a strategic ExCo item
cards.prompt: Put the steps for a strategic ExCo agenda item into a sensible order.
steps: Circulate a short pre-read with the decision needed, options and owner, ahead of the meeting
Open by stating the question, who recommends and who decides
Take the pre-read as read and go straight to debate
Invite challenge and dissent; the most senior person speaks last
Decide, and record the decision and any conditions
Agree the single message every executive will cascade
Track execution at later meetings without reopening the decision

cards.title: Kill the status meeting
cards.body:
If an ExCo meeting is mostly people reading out their numbers, it is a reporting session, not a leadership team.

- **Split the agenda:** a short operating review (exceptions only, dashboards pre-read) and a separate, regular strategic session for the big choices.
- **Shared measures:** give the team two or three company-wide goals that every executive is paid on.
- **One rule:** if a decision is reopened outside the room, bring it back into the room. Never let a one-to-one with the CEO become the real decision forum.

cards.title: Illustration: a bank ExCo writes a charter
cards.body:
Picture a new CEO at a mid-sized regional bank who inherits an executive committee of nine, each running a fiefdom. Decisions drag and the retail and corporate heads do not speak outside meetings.

At an off-site, the team writes a one-page **charter**:

- **Our purpose as a team** (not as functions): three bank-wide priorities for the year.
- **How we decide:** owner recommends, CEO decides on bank-wide issues, ExCo decides on cross-functional ones; decisions are final unless new facts emerge.
- **How we disagree:** in the room, on data, never by message afterwards.
- **How we hold each other to account:** a quarterly peer review where each executive gets candid feedback from colleagues.

The CEO also ties 30% of each executive's bonus to bank-wide results. Charters like this work when the CEO enforces them in the first few meetings; within a year, product approvals speed up and cross-functional launches start landing on time.

cards.question: In ExCo, the CIO says she is 'fine with the plan', but her team later reveals she had serious doubts about the data migration. What does this most strongly suggest about the team?
options: The CIO lacks technical competence
The team needs more frequent status meetings
Leaders do not yet feel safe to voice doubts in the room, so trust and healthy conflict are weak
The decision rights for the project were too clear
cards.explanation: Withholding doubts in the meeting and voicing them elsewhere points to low trust and low psychological safety: people do not believe disagreement is welcome. More status meetings would not fix this; it is a team-health problem, not a competence problem.

cards.title: ExCo table conquered
items: The CEO owns direction, the top team, capital allocation, culture and the board and external relationship; these are hard to delegate.
The CFO is both steward and strategy partner; the COO owns execution; the CHRO owns talent, succession and culture; the CIO makes technology and data work; the CMO owns customer and growth.
Healthy executive teams rest on trust, then healthy conflict, commitment, peer accountability and collective results.
Clear decision rights (recommend, input, agree, decide, execute) end decision churn.
'Disagree and commit': fight in the room, then own the decision in public.
Separate operating reviews from strategic sessions and pay executives partly on company-wide results.

cards.prompt: Think of the most senior team you sit in. Which layer of team health is weakest: trust, conflict, commitment, accountability or collective results? What is one thing you could do in the next meeting to strengthen it?

quiz.question: Which of these is most clearly the CEO's own responsibility rather than another executive's?
options: Designing the monthly management reporting pack
Leading the negotiation with the main packaging supplier, the company's largest single cost contract
Setting overall direction and deciding how major capital is allocated across the business
Choosing the company's cloud hosting provider
quiz.explanation: Direction and major capital allocation across the whole business are central CEO duties. Reporting packs, supplier negotiations and hosting choices belong with the CFO, procurement or operations, and the CIO.

quiz.question: A CFO limits her role to closing the books on time and keeping auditors happy. What is the main value she is leaving on the table?
options: Acting as a strategy partner who tests assumptions and guides capital allocation
Running the plants more efficiently
Owning the company's brand strategy
Managing the leadership succession pipeline
quiz.explanation: Stewardship of reporting and controls is essential, but a modern CFO adds most value by partnering on strategy and capital allocation. Plants, brands and succession belong mainly to the COO, CMO and CHRO.

quiz.question: Which statement about the COO role is most accurate?
options: The COO is always the designated successor to the CEO
Corporate governance codes require every listed company to appoint a COO
The COO is mainly responsible for investor relations and for presenting results to analysts each quarter
The role varies widely but usually centres on reliable execution, often complementing the CEO
quiz.explanation: The COO role is the most variable in the C-suite. It usually centres on execution and is often shaped to complement the CEO. It is not automatically a succession role, is not a legal requirement and is not mainly about investors.

quiz.question: Which activity best shows a CHRO operating at C-suite level?
options: Processing payroll accurately every month
Advising the board's HR and remuneration committee on executive succession and pay
Approving leave requests for head office staff
Organising the annual staff picnic
quiz.explanation: At C-suite level, the CHRO is the steward of leadership talent, succession, reward and culture, and advises the board's HR and remuneration committee. Payroll, leave and events are necessary operational tasks, not the strategic mandate.

quiz.question: After a ransomware attack on a competitor, a director asks who 'owns' cyber risk at your company. What is the best answer?
options: The CIO alone, since it is a technology matter and only the CIO's team has the skills to manage it
The external IT vendor under its service contract
The internal auditor, who tests the controls
The CIO leads the defences, but it is a business risk owned by the CEO, ExCo and the board
quiz.explanation: The CIO leads technical defences, but the consequences of a cyber incident are business-wide, so the CEO, ExCo and board share ownership. Vendors and auditors play roles but do not own the risk.

quiz.question: Tessaly's CMO and CIO are each building their own customer database. What is the best C-suite response?
options: Let both continue so the better one wins
Make the CMO and CIO jointly accountable for one customer-data platform that serves growth goals
Give the whole project to the CIO, because a customer database is fundamentally a technology and data architecture task
Outsource customer data to an agency so neither function owns it
quiz.explanation: Customer insight (the CMO's mandate) and data architecture (the CIO's) depend on each other, so shared accountability for one platform avoids waste and conflicting data. Duplicates waste money; giving it to one side or an agency loses the other's essential input.

quiz.question: In the five-layer model of executive team health, which layer is the foundation that the others rest on?
options: Trust that lets leaders admit mistakes and doubts to each other
Commitment to clear decisions
Peer accountability
Focus on collective results
quiz.explanation: Trust is the base. Without it, leaders avoid open conflict, which weakens commitment, which undermines accountability, and the team drifts towards individual rather than collective results.

quiz.question: After a robust ExCo debate, the CEO decides to close two loss-making depots. The Head of Sales argued against it. Which behaviour shows 'disagree and commit'?
options: Telling his regional managers honestly that the decision was forced on him, while still carrying it out
Raising the issue again with the chairman of the board
Explaining the decision to his team as an ExCo decision he now owns, and helping it succeed
Delaying the closure until the next quarter's results are in
quiz.explanation: Disagree and commit means arguing your case in the room, then owning the decision publicly. Distancing himself, going around the CEO or slow-walking the decision all break collective responsibility.

quiz.question: When assigning decision rights for a major decision, who should hold the 'agree' role, which effectively carries a veto?
options: Only a very small number, such as legal or compliance where a formal requirement applies
Every member of the executive committee
Anyone whose budget or team is materially affected by the decision, so that their interests are protected
The person recommending the decision
quiz.explanation: Veto rights should be rare and tied to formal requirements, otherwise decisions stall. Others give input. Giving every executive or every budget holder a veto recreates the churn decision rights are meant to remove.

quiz.question: Most ExCo time at a telecom company goes to each executive presenting function numbers already in the pre-read. What is the most effective change?
options: Ask each executive to shorten their slides
Split a short, exception-based operating review from a regular strategic session for big decisions
Hold ExCo meetings twice as often
Ask the CEO to review function numbers privately with each executive beforehand, so the meeting is shorter
quiz.explanation: Splitting exception-based operational review from strategic sessions moves leadership time to decisions that need the whole team. Shorter slides or more meetings keep the reporting format, and private one-to-ones push decisions out of the team.

sessions.title: Strategic Decisions Under Uncertainty
sessions.summary: The biggest C-suite decisions are made with half the facts and no second chance. Learn to tell risk from uncertainty, match your process to how reversible a decision is, and use scenarios, pre-mortems, expected value and staged commitments to decide well without pretending to predict the future.
objectives: Distinguish risk from uncertainty and recognise clear, complicated, complex and chaotic situations
Match decision speed and seniority to how reversible and how high-stakes a decision is
Build scenarios around critical uncertainties and run a pre-mortem on a major proposal
Use expected value, base rates and staged commitments while guarding against executive biases

cards.title: An offer with a deadline
cards.setting: CEO's office, Tessaly Foods, Dubai. Rafael is back from his roadshow, and Henrik Vos has joined him.

lines.text: Sunbloom Juices is for sale. Number two juice brand in Brazil. The founders want USD 720 million and a signed term sheet by the end of June. Other bidders are circling.
It's the deal that makes Tessaly a beverages company, not just a dairy. I want it as my last big move.
USD 720 million means heavy borrowing at today's rates. The Brazilian real could move ten percent either way this year. And sugar taxes keep changing in half our markets.
Or we build our own juice line at our Campinas plant for a quarter of the price and grow into it.
(turning to you) Strategy is your job. Recommendation to the board in six weeks. Henrik and I expect a yes.
(later, on a call) Notice the pressure: a deadline, a legacy, a family director. Nobody knows how the next three years will go. How will you decide well when you cannot know?

scenes.heading: Risk is not uncertainty
scenes.narration: With risk, you know the possible outcomes and roughly how likely each is, like default rates on a large loan book. With uncertainty, you cannot reliably list the outcomes or their odds. Most strategic bets live in uncertainty.

scenes.heading: Clear situations
scenes.narration: When cause and effect are obvious, use established practice: sense what is happening, categorise it and respond. Over-analysing a clear situation wastes executive time.

scenes.heading: Complicated situations
scenes.narration: When the answer exists but needs expertise to find, sense, analyse with experts, then respond. A plant capacity study is complicated, not mysterious.

scenes.heading: Complex situations
scenes.narration: When cause and effect only become clear afterwards, such as how consumers will react to a new category, you probe with small safe-to-fail experiments, sense what emerges and then respond.

scenes.heading: Chaotic situations
scenes.narration: When there is no time and no visible pattern, act first to stabilise, then sense and respond. Analysis comes after the bleeding stops.

scenes.heading: The leader's first question
scenes.narration: Before deciding, ask which kind of situation this is. Using an expert study on a complex problem, or experiments in a crisis, is how good leaders make bad calls.

cards.title: How reversible, how big?
cards.caption: Jeff Bezos popularised the 'one-way door' and 'two-way door' language in Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter. Match the process to the decision: treating every decision as irreversible makes a company slow; treating irreversible ones lightly makes it reckless.

items.label: Deliberate at the top
items.detail: High stakes and hard to undo, such as an acquisition: full analysis, dissent invited, board involvement.

items.label: Test and learn fast
items.detail: High stakes but reversible, such as a pricing trial: decide quickly, set limits, watch closely, adjust.

items.label: Check for hidden lock-in
items.detail: Low stakes but hard to undo, such as a long software contract: look for exit costs before signing.

items.label: Delegate and move
items.detail: Low stakes and easy to undo: push the decision down and let teams decide quickly.

cards.title: One-way door or two-way door?
cards.prompt: Sort each Tessaly decision. A one-way door is very hard or costly to reverse; a two-way door can be walked back through cheaply.

items.text: Acquiring Sunbloom Juices for USD 720 million
Testing a new 250 ml pack size in 40 São Paulo shops for a month
Closing the Mombasa chilling centre and selling the land
Changing the wording of a social media campaign
Signing a 15-year exclusive milk-supply contract with a single farm group
Piloting a WhatsApp ordering channel for retailers in one city
Delisting from the stock exchange
Trying a new shift pattern at one plant for six weeks

cards.question: A cyber attack has frozen Tessaly's order system on a Friday evening, trucks are queuing and nobody knows the full extent. Which response fits a chaotic situation?
options: Commission an expert review before taking any action
Act immediately to stabilise, for example isolating systems and switching to manual dispatch, then assess and respond
Run small experiments to see which recovery approach works best
Apply the standard IT ticketing process and wait for the queue
cards.explanation: In chaos, the first job is to act to stabilise, then sense and respond. Expert analysis suits complicated problems, small experiments suit complex ones, and the standard process is for clear situations.

cards.title: Scenario thinking in six moves
cards.caption: Scenarios are not forecasts. They are a set of plausible futures to stress-test a strategy against.

items.label: Frame the focal question
items.detail: For example: should Tessaly enter juices at scale in the next three years, and how?

items.label: List the driving forces
items.detail: Economic, regulatory, consumer, technology and competitor forces that will shape the answer.

items.label: Rank by impact and uncertainty
items.detail: Forces that are predictable go into every scenario. Highly impactful, highly uncertain ones are the critical uncertainties.

items.label: Build the 2x2
items.detail: Take two critical uncertainties as axes and write a short story for each of the four futures.

items.label: Stress-test the options
items.detail: Which option works in most futures? Which fails badly in one? What hedges would help?

items.label: Set signposts
items.detail: Agree early-warning indicators that show which future is unfolding, and the trigger for each next move.

cards.title: Tessaly's four juice futures
cards.caption: Your two critical uncertainties: will currencies and input costs settle in Tessaly's juice markets, and will urban households keep spending on packaged drinks?

items.label: Quiet shelves
items.detail: Stable costs, weak spending. Volume grows slowly; price-led competition. A big acquisition struggles to pay back.

items.label: Golden glass
items.detail: Stable costs, strong spending. Juices boom. Buying scale early looks brilliant.

items.label: Perfect storm
items.detail: Volatile costs, weak spending. Margins crushed. High debt from an acquisition becomes dangerous.

items.label: Premium squeeze
items.detail: Volatile costs, strong spending. Demand holds but imported concentrate prices swing. Pricing power decides winners.

cards.title: Real case: Shell's scenarios and the 1973 oil shock
cards.body:
In the early 1970s, a planning team at Royal Dutch Shell, led by Pierre Wack, stopped relying on single forecasts of oil demand and prices. Instead it built **scenarios**: several plausible futures, including one in which oil-producing countries took more control of supply and prices jumped.

The team's aim was not to predict. It was to change how managers thought, so they would recognise the signs early and know what they would do.

When the **1973 oil crisis** came, prices roughly quadrupled within months. Shell's managers had already rehearsed that world, and the company is widely credited with adapting faster than many rivals. Wack later described the method in two Harvard Business Review articles in 1985, and scenario planning spread to governments and companies worldwide.

**The lesson:** scenarios work when they change decisions today, through prepared responses and **signposts** that tell you which future is arriving.

cards.title: The pre-mortem
cards.setting: Strategy room, Tessaly Foods. You have gathered ExCo and three Sunbloom diligence advisers.

lines.text: You open with an unusual instruction: 'It is three years from now. We bought Sunbloom and it has been a disaster. Take five minutes and write down why it failed.'
We borrowed at the top of the rate cycle, the Brazilian real fell, and our debt covenants tripped in year two.
Sunbloom's two founders left after the earn-out ended, and the distributor network went with them.
(reluctantly) Their biggest modern-trade customer was a single chain. If that contract was not renewed... I had assumed it would be.
In forty minutes the room lists 23 failure reasons. Eleven had never appeared in the investment memo.
That is the point. Imagining failure as a fact makes it safe to voice doubts that people swallow when everyone is excited about a deal.

cards.title: Run a pre-mortem
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a pre-mortem on a major proposal in the right order.
steps: Brief the team on the plan once it is well developed but before it is final
Ask everyone to imagine it is some years later and the plan has failed badly
Each person writes their reasons for the failure independently, in silence
Collect the reasons round the room, starting with the most junior voice
Rank the most likely and most damaging failure causes
Change the plan or add safeguards and signposts to address them

cards.title: Biases that haunt the top floor

cards.front: Overconfidence
cards.back: Executives with strong track records tend to overestimate their odds and underestimate timelines and costs. Counter it with base rates and ranges, not single-point forecasts.

cards.front: Anchoring
cards.back: The first number heard, such as a seller's asking price, pulls every later estimate towards it. Set your own valuation before seeing theirs.

cards.front: Sunk cost and escalation
cards.back: Throwing more money at a failing project because of what has already been spent. Ask: if we were starting today, would we invest the next dollar?

cards.front: Confirmation bias
cards.back: Seeking evidence that supports the deal you already like. Assign someone to build the strongest case against.

cards.front: Groupthink
cards.back: A cohesive senior team drifts to agreement and silences doubts. Counter with independent written views before discussion and the most senior person speaking last.

cards.front: Deference to the most senior voice
cards.back: Once the CEO or chair states a view, debate collapses. Leaders who want real input hold their opinion back until others have spoken.

cards.title: The outside view and staged commitment
cards.body:
**Take the outside view.** Insiders build a plan from their own project's details and are usually too optimistic. Before trusting the plan, ask how a **reference class** of similar decisions turned out: comparable acquisitions, plant builds or launches. Research consistently finds that many acquisitions fail to create value for the buyer, so the burden of proof sits with the deal.

**Buy options, not just assets.** Under deep uncertainty, a smaller first commitment that keeps the right to expand later is often worth more than one big bet:

- a pilot line before a full plant
- a minority stake with a right to buy more
- a phased contract with exit points

The value of staging grows with uncertainty. Each stage needs **pre-agreed triggers**: the signposts that tell you to expand, pause or stop.

cards.title: Real cases: when mega-deals destroyed value
cards.caption: Two famous deals that support taking the outside view on acquisitions. Figures are rounded from widely reported company results and deal terms.

items.label: AOL and Time Warner, agreed 2000
items.detail: Value of the merger when it was announced, at the height of the internet boom.

items.label: AOL Time Warner's 2002 loss
items.detail: A record annual loss, mostly from writing down the goodwill the merger had created.

items.label: Daimler buys Chrysler, 1998
items.detail: Billed as a 'merger of equals' between German and US carmakers.

items.label: Daimler sells Chrysler, 2007
items.detail: Price for about 80% of Chrysler, sold to a private equity firm: a fraction of what was paid.

cards.title: Expected value: buy versus build
cards.caption: Your team's estimates of net present value (NPV) to Tessaly, in USD millions, in three scenarios: upside 25%, base 50%, downside 25%. EV = sum of each outcome times its probability.

items.label: Acquisition worst case
items.detail: In the downside scenario, high debt and lost customers destroy value.

items.label: Staged build worst case
items.detail: A smaller first phase limits the damage if the downside arrives.

cards.question: A new export market has a 40% chance of adding USD 50 million of NPV and a 60% chance of losing USD 20 million. What is its expected value?
options: USD +30 million
USD +8 million
USD +15 million
USD −2 million
cards.explanation: Expected value = (0.4 × 50) + (0.6 × −20) = 20 − 12 = USD +8 million. USD +30 million simply nets 50 against 20 without weighting by probability.

cards.title: The June deadline
cards.situation: Week five. Your analysis shows the staged build has a higher expected value and a far smaller worst case, but the acquisition wins clearly in the 'Golden glass' future. Henrik calls: 'The founders have another bidder. Rafael wants a yes. Put the full USD 720 million offer in the board paper and we will sort out the details after signing.' The board meets in eight days.

choices.text: Recommend the full offer as asked. Rafael is still CEO and the family controls the board.
choices.outcome: You hand the board an irreversible USD 720 million decision framed by a deadline and a seller's price, with the downside analysis buried. When the real falls the next year, directors ask why the pre-mortem findings never reached them.

choices.text: Recommend the staged build, present the acquisition and the scenarios honestly, and propose clear signposts that would justify revisiting Sunbloom later.
choices.outcome: The board sees both options, the expected values and the worst cases. It approves the staged build and asks management to keep a dialogue open with Sunbloom. Henrik is annoyed, but the independent directors note the quality of the paper. You protected the company from a one-way door decided under pressure.

choices.text: Ask for a three-month extension from the founders so you can do more analysis.
choices.outcome: More data will not remove the uncertainty that matters, and the founders refuse. Delay looked like prudence, but it avoided making a recommendation. The board gets no clear advice.

choices.text: Recommend the acquisition but quietly cap your personal support by noting 'strategy has reservations' in the appendix.
choices.outcome: Hiding your real view in an appendix is not candour. If the deal fails, it reads as covering yourself; if it succeeds, it reads as disloyalty. Boards need a clear recommendation and the honest reasoning behind it.

cards.title: Pick the right tool
cards.prompt: Match each decision tool to the moment it serves best.

pairs.right: Testing a ten-year strategy against several very different possible futures
Surfacing hidden reasons a nearly final plan could fail, before committing
Assigning a group to build the strongest possible case against a favoured proposal
Checking a project forecast against how similar projects actually turned out
Investing a smaller amount first while keeping the right to expand when signposts turn
Recording what you knew, expected and decided, to review the quality of the decision later

cards.title: Judge the decision, not just the outcome
cards.body:
Good decisions can turn out badly, and bad decisions can get lucky. Judging a choice only by its result is called **resulting**, and it teaches executives the wrong lessons.

- Keep a **decision journal** for major calls: the options, the information available, your probability estimates, what would change your mind.
- In post-investment reviews, ask two separate questions: *was the process sound given what we knew?* and *what happened?*
- Reward executives for well-made decisions that were unlucky, or they will stop taking sensible risks.

cards.title: How staging works: a cement maker's choice
cards.body:
Picture a cement producer in a fast-growing emerging market, in a period of volatile construction demand. Lenders offer financing for a large new production line, and the controlling shareholder is keen to announce it.

The CFO and strategy head propose a different structure:

- **Stage one:** upgrade an existing line and secure the land and permits for the new one, at about a fifth of the cost.
- **Signposts:** a sustained rise in regional dispatches, a set level of public infrastructure spending and fuel costs within an agreed band.
- **Trigger:** if two of three signposts hold for two quarters, the board approves the full line.

If demand slumps, rivals who built big are left with idle capacity and heavy debt. When demand recovers, the staged company triggers stage two, already holding land and permits. Staging gives up a little upside in exchange for avoiding a potentially severe downside.

cards.question: The CEO opens a strategy discussion by saying, 'I am convinced we should buy this company. Thoughts?' Which change would most reduce the risk of groupthink?
options: Ask everyone to write down their independent view first, and have the CEO share his view last
Keep the meeting short so people do not overthink
Invite only executives who know the target well
Ask the CFO to confirm the numbers support the CEO's view
cards.explanation: Independent written views before discussion, with the most senior person speaking last, protect against anchoring on the CEO and against groupthink. Asking the CFO to confirm the CEO's view invites confirmation bias rather than challenge.

cards.title: Fog bridge crossed
items: Risk has knowable odds; uncertainty does not. Match your approach to clear, complicated, complex or chaotic situations.
Slow down for high-stakes one-way doors; move fast and delegate two-way doors.
Scenarios use two critical uncertainties (high impact, high uncertainty) to stress-test options, with signposts to track which future is unfolding.
A pre-mortem imagines the plan has already failed so that hidden risks can be voiced safely.
Expected value weights each outcome by its probability; also look at the worst case and prefer staged commitments when uncertainty is deep.
Counter overconfidence, anchoring, sunk cost, confirmation and groupthink; judge decisions by their process, not only their outcome.

cards.prompt: Think of a big decision your organisation faces now. Is it a one-way or a two-way door? What are the two most critical uncertainties, and what signpost would tell you early that your plan is going wrong?

quiz.question: What best distinguishes uncertainty from risk in strategic decision-making?
options: Uncertainty only applies to small decisions
Risk involves money, while uncertainty involves people
Risk can always be insured or hedged in the market, whereas uncertainty can never be transferred to anyone
With uncertainty, the possible outcomes or their probabilities cannot be reliably known in advance
quiz.explanation: Risk means the outcomes and their rough odds are knowable, as with a large loan book's default rates. Uncertainty means you cannot reliably list outcomes or their odds, which is typical of strategic bets. Insurability and the money or people split are not the distinction.

quiz.question: The marketing team wants to trial a new price point in 30 Manila shops for one month. How should the C-suite treat this decision?
options: As a one-way door needing a full board paper, since pricing affects the brand's reputation
As a two-way door: delegate it, set limits and let the team move quickly
As a chaotic situation requiring immediate CEO action
As a decision to postpone until the economy stabilises
quiz.explanation: A small, time-limited trial is cheap to reverse, so it is a two-way door that should be delegated and moved on quickly with sensible limits. Escalating it to the board slows the company for no benefit.

quiz.question: When building a scenario 2x2, which driving forces should become the two axes?
options: The two forces the CEO and the strategy team consider most likely to happen
Forces that are highly predictable, so the scenarios are realistic
Forces that are both highly impactful on the question and highly uncertain
Any two forces, as long as one is economic
quiz.explanation: The axes should be the critical uncertainties: forces with high impact and high uncertainty. Predictable forces belong in every scenario rather than on an axis, and choosing by the CEO's view of likelihood defeats the purpose of exploring different futures.

quiz.question: What is the defining instruction in a pre-mortem?
options: Imagine the plan has already failed, and explain why it failed
List everything that could go right with the plan
Review a failed project to find who was responsible
Estimate the probability of success for each option and choose the highest
quiz.explanation: A pre-mortem asks the team to assume the plan has already failed and generate reasons. This makes it safe to voice doubts. Reviewing a past failure is a post-mortem, and probability estimates are a different tool.

quiz.question: A product launch has a 30% chance of adding USD 90 million in NPV, a 50% chance of adding USD 20 million, and a 20% chance of losing USD 100 million. What is its expected value?
options: USD +37 million
USD +3.3 million
USD +17 million
USD +10 million
quiz.explanation: EV = (0.3 × 90) + (0.5 × 20) + (0.2 × −100) = 27 + 10 − 20 = USD +17 million. USD +37 million ignores the downside, and USD +3.3 million is a simple average that ignores the probabilities.

quiz.question: Tessaly has spent USD 12 million on an ERP project that is two years late. The vendor asks for USD 6 million more. The CIO says, 'We can't waste what we have spent.' Which bias is at work, and what question should replace it?
options: Anchoring; the question is what the vendor first quoted
Groupthink; the question is what ExCo agreed originally
Confirmation bias; the question is whether the original business case still supports finishing the project
Sunk cost; the question is whether the next USD 6 million is worth it on its own merits
quiz.explanation: The money already spent is gone whatever you decide, so letting it drive the next decision is the sunk-cost trap. The right test is forward-looking: is the additional investment worth it compared with the alternatives?

quiz.question: Your team forecasts that a new plant will be built in 18 months at budget. What does taking the outside view involve?
options: Asking an external consultant to rebuild the same detailed forecast independently from the project plan
Comparing the forecast with how long similar plant builds actually took and what they cost
Removing all contingency to keep the budget competitive
Asking the plant manager for a more confident estimate
quiz.explanation: The outside view checks your plan against the actual record of a reference class of similar projects, which corrects insider optimism. An external consultant repeating the inside view does not achieve that.

quiz.question: Nobody knows how consumers in Indonesia will react to a new plant-based dairy alternative. How should the leadership team approach it?
options: Probe with small, safe-to-fail experiments, watch what emerges, then scale what works
Commission a detailed expert study of consumer demand, then launch nationally once it is complete
Apply the company's standard launch checklist
Act immediately at full scale to stabilise the market
quiz.explanation: Consumer reaction to a new category is a complex situation: cause and effect only become clear afterwards. Small experiments are the right approach. Expert analysis suits complicated problems, checklists suit clear ones, and act-first suits chaos.

quiz.question: After approving a staged juice-plant investment, what is the main purpose of agreeing signposts?
options: To give the board a reason to cancel the project
To show early which future is unfolding and trigger the agreed next move: expand, pause or stop
To set quarterly sales and margin targets for the juice team that are linked to each investment stage
To replace the need for an annual budget
quiz.explanation: Signposts are early-warning indicators tied to decisions. They tell leaders which scenario is emerging and when to trigger the next stage. They are not targets or a budget substitute.

quiz.question: A CEO made a carefully analysed decision to hedge milk-powder imports. The local currency then strengthened unexpectedly and the hedge cost money. A director calls it 'a bad decision'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because the outcome was a loss
Point out that the hedge was the CFO's decision, so the director should take it up with finance
Promise never to hedge again
Judge it by the process and information available at the time, separately from the outcome
quiz.explanation: Judging decisions only by outcomes ('resulting') punishes sound choices that were unlucky. A good review asks whether the process was sound given what was known, and separately what happened. Blame-shifting or abandoning hedging are poor lessons.
