sessions.title: Boards, Governance and the Tone at the Top
sessions.summary: A CXO answers to a board and sets the ethical weather for thousands of people. Learn what boards do and do not do, how international principles and national codes shape the boardroom, how to handle related-party and conflict situations, and how leaders build or destroy an ethical culture.
objectives: Explain the board's role and the line between governing and managing
Describe the common core of corporate governance codes and how they differ across jurisdictions
Handle related-party transactions and conflicts of interest through proper process
Set an ethical tone at the top and respond to misconduct and whistleblowing fairly

cards.title: Two envelopes
cards.setting: Your office, Tessaly Foods, Dubai. Three days before the quarterly board meeting.

lines.text: One more item for the board pack. Our new East Africa logistics contract should go to Kestrel Haulage. Excellent firm. My brother-in-law runs it. Five years, about USD 40 million.
An hour later, an anonymous email reaches the whistleblowing inbox, copied to you as transformation lead.
It alleges that Gulf region distributors were pushed to take three months of stock in the last week of the quarter, with secret credit extensions, to hit the sales target.
If that is true, revenue is overstated and the quarterly accounts the board approves next week are wrong. The Gulf region reports to Kwame.
It's a malicious complaint from a sacked distributor. Let's not make a drama of it before the board meets. I will look into it myself.
(on the phone) Two envelopes, one test. The board will watch how the next CEO handles a family director's request and a rival's problem. Process, not personalities.

scenes.heading: Stewards for the owners
scenes.narration: The board acts on behalf of all shareholders, including minority ones, and must also weigh employees, customers, lenders and the wider public. In a family-controlled company, protecting minority shareholders is a central duty.

scenes.heading: Strategy and risk
scenes.narration: The board challenges and approves strategy, sets the company's risk appetite and holds management to account for performance against the plan.

scenes.heading: Choosing the CEO
scenes.narration: The board appoints, evaluates, pays and, if needed, removes the chief executive, and it owns CEO succession planning. It is the board's most consequential decision.

scenes.heading: Controls and compliance
scenes.narration: The board makes sure financial reporting is reliable, internal controls work and the company obeys the law, largely through its audit committee.

scenes.heading: Govern, don't manage
scenes.narration: Directors keep their noses in and their hands out: they ask hard questions, approve and oversee, but they do not run the business. Management manages; the board governs.

cards.title: Board versus management
cards.caption: Blurring this line is one of the commonest governance failures, especially in sponsor-led companies.

items.label: CEO
items.right: Leads the executive team under board oversight

items.label: Risk
items.left: Sets appetite and oversees the framework
items.right: Identifies, manages and reports risks daily

items.label: Accounts
items.left: Approves, through the audit committee's review

items.label: Operations
items.right: Runs the business within approved limits

cards.title: Governance codes: the common core
cards.body:
Listed companies are governed by company law, listing rules and usually a **corporate governance code**. The main international reference is the **G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance** (last revised in 2023). Most codes share a core:

- a strong **independent element** on the board
- an **audit committee** of non-executives, chaired by an independent director
- **internal audit** reporting to the audit committee
- review and disclosure of **related-party transactions**
- board evaluation, director training, and attention to board **diversity**

How it is enforced differs:

| Model | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Comply or explain** | UK, Singapore: follow the code or explain why not |
| **Law and listing rules** | US: Sarbanes-Oxley Act and exchange rules |
| **Mostly mandatory** | India, Pakistan: e.g. at least one woman director on listed boards |

Rules and numbers change. Always check the current code where your company is listed.

cards.front: Who should chair the audit committee?
cards.back: An independent director, under most codes. US listing rules go further: every audit committee member must be independent.

cards.front: Can the CEO also chair the board?
cards.back: It depends where you are listed. The UK code expects two people; Pakistan's law requires it for listed companies; in the US combined roles are common, often balanced by a lead independent director.

cards.front: To whom does the head of internal audit report functionally?
cards.back: To the audit committee, as international internal audit standards expect, with the board or committee involved in appointing and removing the head. That lets internal audit report problems about senior managers without fear.

cards.front: What is an independent director for?
cards.back: To bring objective judgement free of ties to management or controlling shareholders, and to protect the interests of all shareholders, including minorities.

cards.front: What does 'comply or explain' mean?
cards.back: Companies follow each code provision or explain publicly why they do not. The idea came from the UK's 1992 Cadbury Report and is now used in many countries.

cards.front: Why do codes expect director training and board evaluation?
cards.back: Boards need current skills on law, risk and their duties, and a regular honest look at how well they work together.

cards.question: Tessaly wants to name Henrik Vos, a founding-family director, as chair of the audit committee. What is the main governance problem?
options: Family directors are not allowed to sit on the board
Governance codes expect the audit committee to be chaired by an independent director, which a founding-family director is not
The audit committee must be chaired by the CFO
The audit committee can only meet once a year
cards.explanation: Most codes expect an independent director to chair the audit committee. A director from the controlling family is non-executive but not independent. The CFO is management and reports to the committee rather than chairing it.

cards.title: Handling a related-party transaction
cards.caption: A related-party deal is not wrong in itself. It becomes a problem when it skips the process that protects minority shareholders.

items.label: Disclose the interest
items.detail: The related director or executive declares the relationship in writing as soon as the deal is proposed.

items.label: Test the terms
items.detail: Management benchmarks price and terms against independent quotes to show they are at arm's length.

items.label: Audit committee review
items.detail: The committee reviews the terms, the evidence and the business case, and makes a recommendation.

items.label: Board decision
items.detail: The board decides; interested directors do not take part in the discussion or vote. Some cases need shareholders' approval.

items.label: Disclose and monitor
items.detail: Record and disclose the transaction as the rules require, and monitor performance against the agreed terms.

cards.title: Real case: Satyam and the family deal (2008–09)
cards.body:
In December 2008 the board of Satyam Computer Services, then one of India's largest IT companies, approved buying two firms controlled by the founder's family, Maytas Properties and Maytas Infra, for about **USD 1.6 billion**. Shareholders protested so strongly that the deal was dropped within a day, and several independent directors resigned in the following weeks.

In January 2009 the chairman, B. Ramalinga Raju, admitted in a letter to the board that the accounts had been falsified for years, including about **USD 1 billion of cash** that did not exist. The government replaced the board, the company was sold to Tech Mahindra later in 2009, and a court convicted Raju in 2015.

India's Companies Act 2013 later tightened the rules on independent directors, audit committees and related-party transactions.

**The lesson:** a related-party deal that skips independent challenge is a red flag. Independent directors must test the terms, not just approve them.

cards.title: A quiet word
cards.setting: A private members' club in Amsterdam. Henrik has invited you to dinner during a visit to the family office.

lines.text: You know the board vote on CEO succession will be close. My family holds 51 percent. Rafael listens to us. So does the HR committee, mostly.
Kestrel Haulage is a family matter. No need for tenders and committees. Put it in the pack as management's recommendation and it will go through quietly.
You check your notes from the logistics review. Two other transporters quoted about 12 percent lower for the same routes.
(next morning) He is testing whether you can be managed. Every CEO candidate here meets this moment. What you do now tells the board who you will be.

cards.title: The Kestrel Haulage request
cards.situation: Henrik wants the USD 40 million logistics contract with his brother-in-law's firm presented as management's recommendation, without the related-party process. Independent quotes are about 12% cheaper. You are on the shortlist for CEO and Henrik's family controls the board. What do you do?

choices.text: Include it as management's recommendation. The family owns the majority and the CEO vote matters.
choices.outcome: The contract goes through. A year later the external auditor flags it as an undisclosed related-party transaction on non-arm's-length terms. The audit committee chair asks who recommended it. Your name is on the paper.

choices.text: Tell Henrik you will take the proposal forward only through the related-party process: written declaration, benchmarked terms, audit committee review and a board decision without him voting. Inform the company secretary.
choices.outcome: Henrik is cold for a week. The audit committee reviews the bids and recommends Kestrel only if it matches the best independent price. Kestrel matches part of it, and the board awards a split contract. Mei Lin tells you later that the independent directors noticed exactly how you handled it.

choices.text: Refuse to put it on the agenda at all, and say nothing to anyone.
choices.outcome: You avoid complicity but leave the issue hanging. Henrik may route it through another executive, and the board never learns a director tried to bypass the process. Silence protects you, not the company.

choices.text: Report Henrik to the securities regulator immediately.
choices.outcome: There has been no breach yet: a proposal was made, and the company's own governance process exists to deal with it. Going straight to the regulator skips the company secretary, the audit committee and the board, and damages trust without first using the internal route.

cards.title: Inside the fraud triangle
cards.prompt: Fraud usually needs pressure, opportunity and a rationalisation. Sort each factor from the Gulf region case into its side of the triangle.

items.text: Regional bonuses pay out only if the quarterly sales target is hit
Credit extensions to distributors need no finance approval below USD 1 million
"Everyone pushes stock at quarter end; it all evens out next quarter"
The COO is publicly competing for the CEO job
Nobody reconciles distributor stock levels with sell-out data
"We are protecting jobs by keeping the numbers up"
Analysts expect revenue growth of 15% this year
Sales managers can change invoice dates in the system

cards.question: Which action by a CEO sends the strongest signal about the company's real ethical standards?
options: Launching a new code of conduct with a town hall
Putting the company's values on posters in every office
How she responds when a top-performing executive is found to have broken the rules
Requiring all staff to sign an annual ethics declaration
cards.explanation: People judge real standards by what leaders do when rules and results collide, especially with high performers. Codes, posters and declarations matter only if behaviour matches them.

cards.title: Handling a whistleblower allegation
cards.prompt: The Gulf region email has arrived. Put the right response in order.
steps: Protect the whistleblower's identity and make clear no retaliation will be tolerated
Secure the evidence: invoices, credit approvals, stock and sell-out data
Route the case to an independent channel, such as the head of internal audit reporting to the audit committee
Investigate independently of the accused's reporting line
Act on the findings consistently, whatever the seniority of those involved, and correct the accounts if needed
Fix the control gaps and share the lessons without naming the whistleblower

cards.title: Who guards what?
cards.prompt: Match each governance role to its main job.

pairs.right: Oversees financial reporting, internal controls, internal audit and the relationship with the external auditor
Reviews senior appointments, executive pay and succession for the board
Independently tests controls and reports findings to the audit committee
Keeps board processes, records and statutory filings in order and advises on governance procedure
Gives an independent opinion on the financial statements to shareholders
Brings objective judgement free of ties to management or the controlling family

cards.title: Real cases: scandals that shaped governance
cards.caption: Most governance rules were written after something went badly wrong. Check which of them apply where you work.

items.label: Cadbury Report, UK
items.detail: After several corporate collapses, a UK committee set out board standards and the 'comply or explain' model.

items.label: OECD Principles published
items.detail: The first international benchmark for corporate governance, now the G20/OECD Principles.

items.label: Enron collapses, US
items.detail: Hidden debts brought down a giant energy trader; its auditor Arthur Andersen also collapsed.

items.label: Sarbanes-Oxley Act, US
items.detail: CEOs and CFOs certify the accounts; independent audit committees; protection for whistleblowers.

items.label: Satyam confession, India
items.detail: Falsified accounts at a leading IT firm; India's Companies Act 2013 followed.

items.label: G20/OECD Principles revised
items.detail: Updated to cover sustainability, shareholder rights and board oversight of risk.

cards.title: Working with your board
cards.body:
- **No surprises.** Bad news goes to the chair early, in person, with what you are doing about it. Directors forgive problems; they rarely forgive learning about them late.
- **Write papers that ask for something.** Lead with the decision needed, then options, risks and your recommendation. Put detail in appendices.
- **Respect the chair's role.** Agree agendas with the chair and do not lobby directors privately to pre-arrange votes.
- **Welcome challenge.** A board that asks hard questions is doing its job. Defensiveness is read as weakness.
- **Never let one director, however powerful, become a back channel around the board.**

cards.title: Real case: Wells Fargo's sales culture (2016)
cards.body:
In September 2016, US regulators fined Wells Fargo about USD 185 million. Employees had opened as many as about 2 million bank and credit-card accounts that customers had not asked for. A later review raised the estimate to about 3.5 million.

The pressure came from the top. The bank had long promoted selling more products to every customer, and branch staff faced demanding daily sales targets. Over several years it had **fired about 5,300 employees** for the practice, but it did not change the targets that drove it.

The CEO resigned in October 2016. In 2020 the bank agreed to pay **USD 3 billion** to settle US criminal and civil investigations, and the Federal Reserve had already capped its growth in 2018.

**The lesson:** punishing junior staff while keeping the incentives that pushed them is not an ethical tone at the top. Leaders own the pressure they create.

cards.question: Kwame offers to look into the Gulf region allegation himself. Why is that a poor choice even if he is completely honest?
options: Because only the external auditor may investigate revenue matters
Because COOs are never allowed to see whistleblowing reports
Because the allegation must first be reported to the police
Because the allegation concerns his own region, so the investigation would not be independent or credible
cards.explanation: An investigation run by the accused's own reporting line cannot be seen as independent, whatever the person's integrity. It should go through an independent channel such as internal audit reporting to the audit committee.

cards.title: Boardroom vault opened
items: The board governs (strategy, risk appetite, CEO appointment and succession, controls) while management manages.

Most codes, guided by the G20/OECD Principles, expect a strong independent element, an independently chaired audit committee and internal audit reporting to it; the rules differ by country, so check yours.
Related-party deals need declaration, arm's-length evidence, audit committee review and a board decision without the interested director.
Fraud needs pressure, opportunity and rationalisation; leaders control more of all three than they think, as Wells Fargo showed.
The tone at the top is set by what leaders reward and tolerate, especially from high performers.
Whistleblowing cases need protection from retaliation and an investigation independent of the accused's line.

cards.prompt: Think of a time when results and rules pulled in different directions in your organisation. What did leaders actually reward? If you had been the CEO, what would you have said and done in the first 24 hours?

quiz.question: A director of a listed company starts phoning plant managers directly to change production schedules. What governance principle is he breaking?
options: The board governs and oversees; management runs day-to-day operations
Directors must not visit company sites
Only executive directors may speak to staff
Production schedules above a certain value must be approved by shareholders in general meeting
quiz.explanation: Directors oversee and challenge but should not run operations. Visiting sites and talking to staff can be healthy; issuing operational instructions bypasses management. Shareholders do not approve production schedules.

quiz.question: Tessaly's board is discussing whether its next CEO should also chair the board. Which statement about international practice is accurate?
options: Every major market bans one person from holding both roles in a listed company
The UK code expects two people, while in the US combined roles are common, often with a lead independent director
Combining the two roles is required in family-controlled companies, so that the family keeps control
Governance codes require the roles to be combined for the first five years after listing
quiz.explanation: Practice differs by market. The UK code expects separate people, and Pakistan's law requires it for listed companies, while in the US combined roles are common and are often balanced by a lead independent director. No major market bans it everywhere or requires it for family firms or new listings.

quiz.question: Under most corporate governance codes, who should chair a listed company's audit committee?
options: The chief financial officer
An independent director
The largest shareholder's nominee
The external auditor's engagement partner
quiz.explanation: Most codes expect an independent director to chair the audit committee, and US listing rules require all its members to be independent. The CFO is management and reports to the committee; a controlling shareholder's nominee is not independent; the external auditor reports to it rather than leading it.

quiz.question: Why does the head of internal audit report functionally to the audit committee rather than to the CEO?
options: Because internal audit is part of the finance function, which in turn reports to the audit committee
Because the CEO is too busy to read audit reports
Because the audit committee pays internal audit staff
So it can report problems, including those involving senior management, without fear
quiz.explanation: The functional reporting line to the audit committee protects internal audit's independence, especially when findings involve senior management. It is not about workload, payroll or placing audit inside finance.

quiz.question: A director's cousin owns a packaging firm bidding for a large Tessaly contract. What should happen to that director when the board decides?
options: Declare the interest and stay out of the discussion and vote
Vote as normal, but only after telling the chair privately about the relationship
Resign from the board before the vote
Chair the discussion, since he knows the firm best
quiz.explanation: An interested director must declare the interest and not take part in the discussion or vote. Telling the chair privately is not enough, resignation is not required, and leading the discussion would be a clear conflict.

quiz.question: Which statement about rules on gender diversity on listed company boards is accurate?
options: International codes discourage any quotas or targets for board diversity and leave it to shareholders
Only the US sets a legal requirement for women on listed company boards, through its listing rules
India and Pakistan require at least one woman director on listed boards
Gender diversity rules apply only to state-owned companies, never to listed ones
quiz.explanation: Some jurisdictions make board diversity a legal requirement: India and Pakistan, for example, require at least one woman director on listed company boards. International codes encourage attention to diversity rather than discouraging it, and the rules are not limited to the US or to state-owned firms.

quiz.question: A sales manager tells himself, 'The company underpays me anyway, so moving a few invoices is only fair.' Which part of the fraud triangle does this show?
options: Pressure
Opportunity
Detection
Rationalisation
quiz.explanation: Telling yourself the act is fair or justified is rationalisation. Pressure is the financial or performance need; opportunity is the weak control that allows the act. Detection is not one of the three sides.

quiz.question: A star regional head is found to have bullied staff and backdated invoices, but his region delivers the best results. What will most shape how employees see the company's real values?
options: Whether the code of conduct is reissued that month with a stronger section on conduct
Whether he faces the same consequences as anyone else would
Whether the CEO mentions ethics in the next town hall
Whether HR runs refresher training for his region
quiz.explanation: Employees read real standards from how leaders treat high performers who break rules. If he is protected, every code and speech is undermined. Training and messages help only when consequences are consistent.

quiz.question: An allegation of channel stuffing involves the COO's own region. Who should run the investigation?
options: The COO, because he knows the region best
The regional sales head, supervised by the COO, since they have the fastest access to the data
The marketing team, as it has the distributor data
An independent function such as internal audit, reporting to the audit committee
quiz.explanation: Investigations must be independent of the accused's reporting line. Internal audit, reporting to the audit committee, gives that independence. The COO, his regional head or another business function cannot provide it credibly.

quiz.question: You need board approval for a major capital project. How should your board paper open?
options: With a detailed history of the project since it was first discussed, so directors have full context
With all the supporting spreadsheets so directors can do their own analysis
With the decision being asked for, then the options, key risks and your recommendation
With a summary of every ExCo member's personal view
quiz.explanation: Good board papers lead with the decision required and give options, risks and a clear recommendation, with detail in appendices. Histories and raw spreadsheets bury the ask, and the board needs management's recommendation rather than a list of opinions.

sessions.title: Crisis, Culture, Presence and Succession
sessions.summary: The top job is tested in the storm. Learn to lead a crisis and talk to staff, regulators, investors and the public, to shape culture and keep a transformation alive, to show executive presence under pressure, and to own succession and your own growth as a CXO.
objectives: Lead the first hours and days of a crisis and communicate with each stakeholder group
Communicate with investors and the market under international disclosure principles
Shape culture through the levers leaders control and keep transformation going through the dip
Build executive presence and plan succession and your own development as a CXO

cards.title: 6:12 am
cards.setting: Your phone in a Nairobi hotel room, before dawn. Forty unread messages.

lines.text: A video is spreading fast: a mother in Nairobi holds a carton of Tessaly strawberry milk and says three children on her street fell sick after drinking it.
The share price will open under pressure. Two analysts have already messaged asking if we are recalling. What do we say?
The batch code is from our Nairobi plant, last Tuesday. Plant tests were clean. This smells like a cold-chain failure somewhere in the market.
I want a statement out in one hour: 'Tessaly products are 100 percent safe.' We cannot look weak.
And nobody talks to the media except Rafael. This is the family's name too.
(calling) Rafael has asked you to lead the crisis team. This is the last stage before the board decides. Breathe. People first, then facts, then words.

scenes.heading: People first
scenes.narration: Start with safety. Who might be harmed, and what will stop more harm now? A precautionary hold on a suspect batch costs money. A second wave of sick children costs everything.

scenes.heading: Facts before adjectives
scenes.narration: Set up a small crisis team with one leader. Separate what you know, what you do not know, and what you are doing to find out. Never claim certainty you do not have.

scenes.heading: Speak early, with one voice
scenes.narration: Silence gets filled by rumours. Communicate early through one trained spokesperson, show you care, say what you are doing and when you will update next.

scenes.heading: Regulators and the market
scenes.narration: Brief the food authority and other regulators yourself before they hear it elsewhere. If the news is price-sensitive, the stock exchange must hear it through the formal channel, not analysts first.

scenes.heading: A steady rhythm
scenes.narration: Hold the team to a fixed cycle of meetings and updates. Staff, distributors and customers need to hear from you as often as the media do.

scenes.heading: Recover and learn
scenes.narration: Once stable, fix the root cause, support the people affected and run an honest review. The best leaders come out of a crisis with stronger systems and more trust.

cards.title: The crisis leadership cycle
cards.caption: Every crisis ends with lessons that should improve preparation for the next one.

items.label: Prepare
items.detail: Crisis plan, trained team and spokesperson, contact lists, scenario drills.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Protect people, establish facts, take control of communication, decide fast.

items.label: Recover
items.detail: Fix the root cause, restore operations, rebuild trust with each stakeholder.

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Honest review without blame, update plans, controls and training.

cards.title: The 100 percent statement
cards.situation: It is 7:30 am. Rafael wants the statement 'Tessaly products are 100 percent safe' published now. Test results from the batch will take 36 hours. The national food-safety regulator has collected samples. The batch went to about 600 shops around Nairobi. Analysts are calling Layla. You lead the crisis team. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Publish Rafael's statement. Confidence protects the brand and the share price.
choices.outcome: By evening the regulator says testing is under way, and the media contrast it with your '100 percent safe' claim. If a single sample fails, your credibility is gone for years. Certainty you do not have is the costliest thing a leader can say.

choices.text: Put a precautionary hold on the batch, say what is known and not known, explain the testing with the regulator, commit to the next update time, and make any price-sensitive disclosure through the stock exchange first.
choices.outcome: Within hours, distributors pull the batch and families see a company acting responsibly. The market gets the same information at the same time through the exchange. When tests come back, you are believed. Mei Lin writes: 'That was a CEO's call.'

choices.text: Say nothing until the test results arrive in 36 hours.
choices.outcome: Silence for a day and a half lets the video define the story. Rumours of a cover-up spread on social media, and more children may drink the batch. Waiting for complete facts is not caution in a crisis.

choices.text: Brief the two analysts privately that it is probably a market cold-chain problem, to steady the share price.
choices.outcome: You calm the market for an hour, but you have given selected people price-sensitive information before the public. That creates a serious disclosure problem and helps nobody who may be at risk.

cards.title: Morning of the crisis
cards.prompt: Put the crisis team's first actions in a sensible order.
steps: Put a precautionary hold on the suspect batch and trace where it went
Convene the crisis team with one leader and one spokesperson
Brief the food-safety regulator and agree testing
Issue a holding statement: concern, actions taken, what is unknown, next update time
Make any required disclosure to the stock exchange before speaking to analysts
Brief staff and distributors so they hear it from the company
Hold regular update cycles until the facts are established

cards.title: Who needs what from you?
cards.caption: Map stakeholders by their power over the outcome and their interest in it, then set how closely you engage each one.

items.label: Keep satisfied
items.detail: High power, lower interest: for example lenders. Brief them proactively so concern does not turn into action.

items.label: Manage closely
items.detail: High power, high interest: the food-safety regulator, the board, major shareholders. Engage personally and often.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Low power, low interest: watch for changes, light-touch updates.

items.label: Keep informed
items.detail: Lower power, high interest: staff, distributors, affected families. Communicate regularly and with empathy.

cards.question: During the crisis, a fund manager phones Layla and asks whether Tessaly expects a material write-off. Nothing has been disclosed to the market yet. What should Layla do?
options: Give an honest private estimate, since he is a long-term investor
Say nothing beyond what is already public, and make sure any price-sensitive information is first disclosed through the stock exchange
Tell him the company expects no write-off, to protect the share price
Refer him to Henrik as the family representative
cards.explanation: Price-sensitive information must reach the whole market through the exchange, not selected investors first. A private estimate is selective disclosure; a reassuring guess could mislead the market; a family director is not a disclosure channel.

cards.title: Real cases: two product-safety crises
cards.caption: Two of the most studied safety crises. One company put people first; the other's delay became a national scandal.

items.label: What happened
items.left: Seven people died after taking capsules someone had laced with cyanide in shops
items.right: Suppliers added melamine to milk; about 300,000 infants fell ill and at least six died

items.label: First move
items.left: Johnson & Johnson warned the public and recalled about 31 million bottles nationwide
items.right: Complaints began in late 2007; the public was told only in September 2008

items.label: Communication
items.left: Open and frequent, led by senior leaders; tamper-evident packs followed
items.right: Delay; the full scale emerged only after national authorities stepped in

items.label: Outcome
items.left: The brand regained much of its market share within about a year
items.right: Sanlu went bankrupt and its former chair was sentenced to life in prison

cards.title: Talking to investors and the market
cards.body:
Listed-company CXOs speak to the market under rules. The principles are shared worldwide, and IOSCO, the global body of securities regulators, sets them out:

- **Price-sensitive (inside) information** must be disclosed promptly through the official channel, so all investors get it at the same time. Examples: the EU and UK Market Abuse Regulation, and the continuous-disclosure rules of exchanges in Singapore, India, Pakistan and elsewhere. In the US, **Regulation FD** stops companies briefing analysts or favoured investors selectively.
- **Insider dealing** is banned almost everywhere: nobody may trade on, or tip others about, unpublished price-sensitive information. Companies set **closed periods** around results.

Beyond the rules, credibility comes from **consistency**: one clear equity story, guidance you can meet, bad news delivered as early and plainly as good news, and the same message to investors, staff and regulators.

Details and timings differ by market: check the rules everywhere your shares are listed.

cards.title: The chiller nobody fixed
cards.setting: Crisis room, Nairobi, day three. The test results are in.

lines.text: Plant samples are clean. The problem was a distributor's cold store on the edge of the city. Its chiller failed for two days and stock was sold anyway.
The regulator agrees. We have recalled what remained and are paying for the children's treatment. The share price is recovering.
Then a regional supervisor, Wanjiru, asks to speak. Her hands are shaking.
She had reported the failing chiller in the regional chat group two weeks earlier. Her manager replied: 'Not now. Quarter end. Push the stock.'
The chiller is the cause. The culture is the root cause. People here learned that hitting the number matters more than raising a problem.
(quietly) I built that rule. 'Never miss a quarter.' I said it at every conference for nineteen years.

cards.title: Three levels of culture
cards.caption: What you can see sits on top of what people say they value, which rests on what they actually believe. Change the bottom, or nothing lasts.

items.label: Artefacts
items.detail: Visible things: offices, dress, slogans, rituals, processes, the way meetings run.

items.label: Espoused values
items.detail: What the organisation says it values: the code, the posters, the strategy document.

items.label: Underlying assumptions
items.detail: Unspoken beliefs people act on without thinking, such as 'never bring bad news at quarter end'.

cards.title: Which level of culture?
cards.prompt: Sort each observation from Tessaly into the level of culture it belongs to.

items.text: A 'Quality First' banner over the plant gate
The code of conduct states that safety comes before sales
Staff silently believe that raising a problem at quarter end harms your career
Executives have reserved parking next to the entrance
The annual report says the company values openness
People assume that the CEO's view is final, whatever the evidence
Monthly town halls run as presentations with no questions
The strategy deck lists 'customer obsession' as a core value

cards.question: Which leadership action is most likely to change the assumption that 'bad news at quarter end harms your career'?
options: Adding 'openness' to the list of company values
Publicly thanking and protecting Wanjiru, and changing incentives so safety and quality issues can stop a sale without penalty
Running an awareness poster campaign on speaking up
Asking HR to update the whistleblowing policy wording
cards.explanation: Underlying assumptions change when people see leaders reward the behaviour they claim to want, and when systems such as incentives back it up. Values lists, posters and policy wording work only at the artefact and espoused levels.

cards.title: Keeping a transformation alive
cards.body:
A crisis often exposes why a company needs to transform. Leading that transformation from the C-suite means:

- **A case for change people believe:** a 'burning platform' creates urgency, but a 'burning ambition' sustains it. Use both.
- **A united top team:** if executives disagree in private, middle managers will notice within days.
- **Few priorities, clearly sequenced:** a transformation office tracks a handful of initiatives, not fifty.
- **Expect the dip:** performance often falls before it improves as people learn new ways of working, the **J-curve**. Leaders who panic in the dip abandon change just before it pays off.
- **Lead indicators, not just results:** track adoption, behaviours and capability as well as profit.
- **Visible symbols:** what leaders stop doing, measure and celebrate tells people the change is real.

cards.title: Real case: Uber resets its culture (2017)
cards.body:
In February 2017 a former Uber engineer, Susan Fowler, published an account of sexual harassment and of HR failing to act. Other complaints about the company's aggressive culture followed.

The board commissioned an independent review led by former US Attorney General Eric Holder; its recommendations, published in June 2017, covered leadership, HR, board oversight and the company's values. That same month co-founder Travis Kalanick resigned as CEO under pressure from major investors.

In August 2017 the board chose an **external** successor, Dara Khosrowshahi from Expedia. He replaced the old list of values with new cultural norms, including **"We do the right thing. Period."**, and took Uber to a stock market listing in 2019.

**The lesson:** the old values had celebrated growth at almost any cost, and behaviour followed. Changing culture took new leaders, new norms and new board oversight, not only a new poster.

cards.front: Presence means being the loudest voice in the room.
cards.back: Myth. Presence is composure, clarity and credibility. Often the most senior person speaks least and is listened to most.

cards.front: Under pressure, people watch the leader's face before they hear the words.
cards.back: Fact. Visible calm in a crisis gives people permission to think clearly. Panic spreads faster than any memo.

cards.front: A CXO should open with the background and build up to the point.
cards.back: Myth. Senior audiences want the bottom line first, then the reasons and the ask. Background goes last, if at all.

cards.front: Presence can be learned.
cards.back: Fact. It is built from preparation, feedback, practice and self-awareness, not only personality.

cards.front: Admitting 'I don't know yet' weakens executive presence.
cards.back: Myth. Saying what you don't know, and how you will find out, builds credibility. Bluffing destroys it.

cards.front: Presence is the same as being polished.
cards.back: Myth. Polish without substance or authenticity is quickly spotted by boards and staff alike.

cards.title: Internal or external CEO successor?
cards.caption: Boards weigh both. A strong internal pipeline gives the board a real choice rather than a forced one.

items.label: Knowledge
items.left: Knows the business, people and culture deeply
items.right: Brings fresh perspective and outside experience

items.label: Risk
items.left: Known track record lowers selection risk
items.right: Higher risk of poor cultural fit

items.label: Change
items.left: May be too attached to the old ways

items.label: Continuity
items.right: Disruption and possible exits of internal candidates

cards.title: Succession and self-development terms
cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Who steps in at once, on an interim basis, if the CEO is suddenly unable to continue
A candidate who could take the role today with acceptable risk
A talent tool that plots current performance against future potential
A strength overused or a blind spot that can stall a senior career, such as arrogance or micromanaging
A small trusted group outside your reporting line who give you candid counsel
A confidential professional who helps a leader see their patterns and change behaviour

cards.title: The last stage
cards.setting: Board lounge, Dubai, one month later. The HR and remuneration committee will interview both candidates next week.

lines.text: I owe you something. The '100 percent' statement would have been my last mistake. Whatever the board decides, I'm proud of how you led this year.
And I owe you a thank-you for keeping the Gulf region review fair. It was ugly, but I would rather it came out this way.
You were difficult over Kestrel. You were also right. The family wants a CEO the other shareholders trust.
Next week the committee will test everything: your styles, your team, your decisions, the board, the crisis and yourself. One question will be about your own development.
At the top, nobody gives you honest feedback unless you build ways to get it. Tell them how you will. Then go and earn the corner office.

cards.title: Growing when nobody tells you the truth
cards.body:
The higher you rise, the less honest feedback you receive. People filter bad news and laugh at your jokes.

- **Build feedback channels on purpose:** a confidential 360 every year or two, skip-level meetings, and a direct report whose job includes telling you what others will not.
- **Know your derailers:** your greatest strength overused is often your biggest risk.
- **Use outside counsel:** an executive coach and a small personal board of advisers outside the company.
- **Develop your successor early.** Leaders who make themselves replaceable are the ones boards trust with bigger roles.
- **Protect your energy:** sleep, family and faith are not luxuries; tired leaders make worse decisions.

cards.question: In a board interview, a CEO candidate is asked about her development needs. Which answer shows the most self-awareness?
options: "My weakness is that I work too hard and care too much about results."
"My 360 shows that under pressure I tend to take decisions back from my team. I now agree decision rights up front and have a coach working with me on it."
"I don't think I have significant development needs at this stage."
"My team would say I am very demanding, but that is what makes us successful."
cards.explanation: Strong self-awareness names a real derailer with evidence and shows concrete steps to manage it. The other answers either disguise a strength as a weakness, deny any needs or justify the problem.

cards.title: Storm deck mastered
items: In a crisis: people first, facts before claims, one voice, early and regular communication, regulators briefed directly.
Price-sensitive news goes to the whole market through the stock exchange first; never brief selected investors or analysts ahead of it.
Culture lives at three levels: artefacts, espoused values and underlying assumptions; leaders change it through what they reward, tolerate and model.
Transformation needs a believable case, a united top team, few priorities and the nerve to hold through the J-curve.
Executive presence is composure, clarity and credibility, and it can be learned.
The board owns CEO succession; a strong CXO builds successors and deliberate feedback channels for their own growth.

cards.prompt: Imagine you are interviewed for a C-suite role next month. What crisis would you describe, what did it teach you, and what is the one derailer you would admit to, with the evidence and what you are doing about it?

quiz.question: A video claims a Tessaly product made children sick. What should the leadership team prioritise first?
options: Protecting the share price with a strong statement
Protecting people from further harm and establishing the facts
Identifying which manager is to blame
Preparing the legal defence against possible claims from the affected families
quiz.explanation: People's safety and the facts come first. A strong statement without facts can backfire, blame comes later through a proper review, and legal preparation matters but cannot lead the response.

quiz.question: Test results will take 36 hours. What should the company's first public statement include?
options: What is known, what is not yet known, what the company is doing, and when it will update next
A firm assurance that all products are completely safe, to stop panic spreading on social media
No comment until the results are available
A suggestion that a competitor may have started the video
quiz.explanation: A good holding statement is honest about what is and is not known, shows action and sets the next update. False certainty, silence and blaming others all damage trust.

quiz.question: A listed company's CFO learns of a major product recall that is likely to affect its profits materially. What should happen before she discusses it with any analyst?
options: She should check with the largest shareholder first
Nothing special; analysts may be briefed as long as they promise to keep it confidential
The information should be disclosed to the stock exchange through the formal channel
The recall should be kept confidential until the annual report
quiz.explanation: Price-sensitive information must be disclosed promptly through the stock exchange so all investors receive it together. Briefing a shareholder or analysts first is selective disclosure; waiting until the annual report is not prompt disclosure.

quiz.question: On a power-interest map, how should the crisis team engage the national food-safety regulator, which has high power over the outcome and high interest in it?
options: Monitor and send occasional updates
Keep satisfied with a formal quarterly briefing from the company secretary
Keep informed through the company website
Manage closely, with direct and frequent senior engagement
quiz.explanation: High power with high interest calls for close management: direct, frequent and senior. 'Keep satisfied' fits high power with lower interest, and 'keep informed' fits high interest with lower power.

quiz.question: Which is an example of the deepest level of organisational culture?
options: The company's values printed on staff ID cards
A shared, unspoken belief that disagreeing with senior managers is dangerous
The open-plan design of the head office
The code of conduct's statement that integrity is the company's most important value
quiz.explanation: Underlying assumptions are the unspoken beliefs people act on, and they are the deepest level. Office design and printed values are visible artefacts; the code's statements are espoused values.

quiz.question: A CEO wants to build a culture where problems are raised early. Which action will have the most impact?
options: Adding 'transparency' to the company's values
Sending a personal CEO email to all staff encouraging them to speak up about problems early
Holding a training session on communication skills
Visibly rewarding people who raise problems and never penalising the bearer of bad news
quiz.explanation: Culture follows what leaders reward, tolerate and model. Visibly rewarding early warnings changes beliefs about what is safe. Values, emails and training help only if behaviour and consequences back them up.

quiz.question: Six months into a sales-force transformation, productivity has dipped as staff learn new tools. A director wants to cancel it. What should the leader explain?
options: That the dip proves the transformation was poorly designed and should be reworked before going further
That results should be ignored during any transformation
That a temporary dip is common while people learn (the J-curve); lead indicators show if it is on track
That cancelling would be cheaper than continuing
quiz.explanation: Performance often falls before it improves during change. The right response is to check lead indicators such as adoption and capability, not to panic or ignore results. A dip alone does not prove poor design.

quiz.question: Which behaviour best demonstrates executive presence when briefing a board during a crisis?
options: Calmly giving the bottom line first, admitting what is not yet known and stating the decisions needed
Speaking at length to show command of every detail
Projecting complete certainty about the outcome so directors stay calm and do not over-react to the news
Letting each team member present their own part to share the credit
quiz.explanation: Presence is composure, clarity and credibility: the bottom line first, honesty about unknowns and a clear ask. Long detail and false certainty undermine credibility, and fragmenting the briefing loses the clear leadership voice the board needs.

quiz.question: Who owns CEO succession planning in a listed company?
options: The outgoing CEO, who knows the business and the candidates better than anyone else on the board
The CHRO alone
The largest shareholder
The board, usually through a committee such as HR and remuneration, supported by the CHRO
quiz.explanation: Appointing the CEO is the board's decision and succession is its responsibility, typically through a board committee supported by the CHRO. The outgoing CEO contributes but must not control it, and a shareholder acts through the board.

quiz.question: A CFO known for brilliant analysis now insists on checking every number personally, and her team has stopped taking initiative. What is this an example of?
options: A healthy control environment, since the CFO is personally accountable for every number
A derailer: a strength overused until it becomes a weakness
An emergency succession risk
A transformational leadership behaviour
quiz.explanation: Her analytical strength, overused as micromanagement, has become a derailer that stifles her team. Strong controls are designed into processes, not done by one person checking everything.

bank.question: A new CEO, formerly a top strategy consultant, rewrites her executives' board papers late at night and personally reworks their financial models. Results are fine, but two strong executives say they feel 'like analysts again'. Which style is she overusing, and what is the best corrective?
options: Commanding; she should keep tight control but explain the reasons behind each of her instructions more carefully
Affiliative; she should focus less on relationships and more on results
Pacesetting; she should agree standards and outcomes up front and coach to the gap rather than redo the work
Democratic; she should take more decisions herself instead of consulting
bank.explanation: Redoing work to her own standard is pacesetting, which damages climate when sustained with senior people. The fix is to agree the standard and outcome in advance and coach the gap. Commanding is about orders, not redoing work, and she is not over-consulting or over-focusing on relationships.

bank.question: After a bank merger, staff from the two legacy banks are openly hostile following painful layoffs. The board-approved direction for the merged bank has already been set and communicated clearly. Which style should the new CEO lean on most in the next few months?
options: Affiliative, to heal the damage and rebuild trust between the two groups
Visionary, to set out an inspiring new direction that unites both legacy groups around one future
Pacesetting, to show both groups the standard expected
Commanding, to stop the conflict quickly
bank.explanation: When trust is broken and wounds need healing, the affiliative style fits. The direction is already clear, so more visionary effort is not the main need. Pacesetting and commanding would deepen resentment in a non-emergency.

bank.question: Your CHRO, a highly respected HR leader, has just been asked to also run Tessaly's procurement function for a year, something she has never done. She is excited about it. Using situational leadership, how should you lead her on procurement in the first months?
options: Delegating, because she is a senior and proven executive who will resent close supervision
Supporting, because experienced leaders mainly need encouragement
Coaching, because her commitment is likely to be low
Directing, with clear goals, context and frequent early check-ins on this new task
bank.explanation: Situational leadership is task-specific. On procurement her competence is low but her commitment is high, which calls for directing at first. Her seniority in HR does not transfer automatically, so delegating would be premature; her commitment is high, so coaching and supporting do not fit yet.

bank.question: During a cost crisis, a CEO cuts her own salary and perks first, travels economy like everyone else and keeps her promises to staff even when it costs her. Which element of transformational leadership does this best illustrate?
options: Intellectual stimulation
Idealised influence
Individualised consideration
Contingent reward
bank.explanation: Idealised influence is leading as a role model whose conduct people admire and want to follow. Intellectual stimulation is about challenging assumptions, individualised consideration about attention to each person's needs, and contingent reward is a transactional exchange.

bank.question: A CFO pays little attention to finance operations until internal audit or the external auditor reports a problem, then acts firmly to fix it. In the full range of leadership, how is this best described?
options: Laissez-faire, because she avoids involvement altogether
Passive management by exception, because she steps in only once problems surface
Active management by exception, because she corrects deviations from standards firmly once she knows of them
Contingent reward, because she corrects performance
bank.explanation: Stepping in only after problems are reported is passive management by exception. Active management by exception would involve monitoring for deviations before they surface. She does act when problems appear, so this is not laissez-faire, and she is not exchanging rewards for delivery.

bank.question: The board is comparing two CEO candidates with similar results. Candidate A is magnetic on stage and credits his own vision for every success. Candidate B is reserved, credits her team publicly, takes blame for failures and has twice made very tough calls to protect the company's long-term health. Based on research into leaders of companies that went from good to great, which profile is more promising?
options: Candidate A, because visible charisma and a strong personal brand are the main drivers of long-term performance
Neither, because results are equal so profile does not matter
Candidate A, because a CEO must be the company's public face
Candidate B, because she combines personal humility with strong professional will
bank.explanation: The research found that leaders of lasting high performers combined humility (credit to others, ambition for the company) with intense resolve to do what was needed. Charisma was not the distinguishing factor, and how results are achieved matters for sustaining them.

bank.question: In town halls, Tessaly's CEO checks his phone while staff ask questions. Six months later, regional managers do the same in their own meetings, and engagement scores on 'my manager listens to me' have fallen. What concept best explains this?
options: The shadow of the leader: people copy what senior leaders do far more than what they say
Groupthink: the managers are copying each other and agreeing too quickly on how to run meetings
Laissez-faire leadership by the regional managers
Management by exception: managers only listen when there is a problem
bank.explanation: Senior leaders' everyday behaviour casts a shadow that is copied down the organisation. Groupthink is about decision-making, and while the managers' behaviour may look disengaged, the cause shown here is imitation of the CEO's example.

bank.question: Eighteen months ago a CEO took over a loss-making textile mill and used a commanding style to save it. The mill is now stable and profitable, but managers wait for instructions and several capable ones have left. What is the best advice to him?
options: Continue commanding, because it has been proven to work at this mill
Switch to laissez-faire so managers are forced to take initiative
Shift towards visionary, coaching and democratic styles now the crisis is over, and say so openly
Replace the remaining managers with people who are comfortable working under a strong, directive leader
bank.explanation: Commanding fits a genuine turnaround but damages climate once the crisis passes. Shifting to climate-building styles, and naming the shift, lets managers take ownership again. Laissez-faire is absence of leadership, not empowerment, and replacing managers treats the symptom.

bank.question: A new CEO joins a pharma company whose staff are capable and committed but confused: the old strategy has clearly failed and nobody knows where the company is heading. There is no immediate emergency. Which style should come first?
options: Coaching, to develop each executive's skills so they can work out the new direction themselves
Affiliative, to make people feel valued
Pacesetting, to show what high performance looks like
Visionary, to set a clear new direction and show each person's part in it
bank.explanation: When people are capable but lack direction, the visionary style is most powerful: it sets the destination and leaves room for how. Coaching and affiliative styles help later or in other situations, and pacesetting would add pressure without direction.

bank.question: Your Head of Treasury is expert and confident at managing bank lines, which she has done for ten years, but she is new to and anxious about presenting to the board's risk committee. How should you lead her?
options: Directing on both tasks, to be consistent
Delegating on bank lines, and more direction and support on board presentations
Delegating on both tasks, because she is a senior expert
Supporting on bank lines to keep her motivated, and delegating board presentations to build her confidence
bank.explanation: Situational leadership is applied task by task. On bank lines she is skilled and committed, so delegate. On board presentations her competence and confidence are low, so she needs direction and support. One style for both tasks ignores the difference.

bank.question: A newly promoted COO tells his plant heads, 'Our job is to protect operations from the rest of ExCo.' He wins every budget argument for operations, while company-wide priorities such as digital ordering stall. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: He is still treating his function as his first team, instead of the executive team and the enterprise
He is using an affiliative style with his plant heads
He needs clearer decision rights over the digital budget so that operations' needs are properly protected
He is applying healthy conflict in ExCo
bank.explanation: A C-suite leader's first team is the executive team, and their job is enterprise results. Defending his function against peers shows he has not made that shift. More decision rights would amplify the problem, and winning every fight for one function is not healthy conflict.

bank.question: At a listed company, the CEO pressures the CFO to 'find' USD 8 million of extra profit before year end by changing provisioning assumptions without new evidence. What should the CFO do?
options: Agree, since the CEO is accountable for results
Make the change, but disclose the revised provisioning assumptions fully and clearly in the notes to the accounts
Resign immediately without raising it with anyone
Decline, explain why the change is unsupportable, and raise it with the audit committee chair if pressed
bank.explanation: The CFO's stewardship of reporting integrity is non-negotiable, and the audit committee relies on it. A note does not cure an unsupported change. Resigning without raising it leaves the problem in place; the right path is to refuse and escalate to the audit committee if needed.

bank.question: At a telecom company, each executive is paid only on their function's KPIs. The CMO launches campaigns that the network cannot support, and the CTO delays upgrades marketing depends on. Which change addresses the root cause most directly?
options: Ask the CEO to settle each dispute as it arises, so that the network and marketing plans stay aligned in practice
Tie a real share of every executive's reward to shared company goals and make cross-functional priorities joint
Hold a team-building retreat
Hire a programme manager to coordinate marketing and technology
bank.explanation: When incentives reward only functional results, executives optimise their silos. Shared goals and joint accountability align them with collective results. CEO refereeing, retreats and coordinators treat symptoms while leaving the incentives untouched.

bank.question: In ExCo meetings, every proposal is accepted politely and nobody challenges anyone. Afterwards, executives complain about each other to the CEO in private. Which layer of team health should the CEO work on first?
options: Collective results, by publishing a company scorecard
Peer accountability, by asking executives to call each other out
Trust, so that leaders feel safe enough to disagree openly in the room
Commitment, by asking everyone to sign off decisions in writing
bank.explanation: Artificial harmony in the room and complaints outside it signal fear of conflict sitting on weak trust. The layers above depend on the base, so building trust comes first. Scorecards, written sign-offs and peer accountability will not hold without it.

bank.question: The decision to centralise procurement at a food group has been reopened four times. Each time, a different executive says they were 'never really consulted' or 'thought they had a veto'. What is the best fix?
options: Give every executive a formal veto so that all are bought in
Let the CEO decide alone and announce it without further discussion, since consultation has already failed
Before the next round, agree who recommends, who gives input, who (if anyone) must agree, and who decides
Commission a consultant to make the decision
bank.explanation: The churn comes from unclear decision rights. Agreeing roles up front means people know whether they are giving input or deciding. Universal vetoes create gridlock, a CEO decision without input loses expertise and buy-in, and consultants cannot own the decision.

bank.question: After ExCo decides to exit a loss-making product line, the CMO, who argued against it, tells his brand managers, 'This was finance's decision. I fought it.' What is the main damage this does?
options: It undermines collective responsibility, so the decision is weakened and the team appears divided
It breaches the company's disclosure rules
It is fine, because honesty with your team matters more
It shows he lacks marketing competence
bank.explanation: Once decided, executives should own the decision publicly. Distancing himself signals division, invites resistance and weakens execution. Honesty means arguing in the room, not undermining the decision afterwards. It is not a disclosure or competence matter.

bank.question: A board member says, 'Our COO is obviously our next CEO; that is what COOs are for.' What is the most accurate response?
options: Agree; the COO role exists to prepare the CEO successor
Disagree; COOs are prohibited from becoming CEO in listed companies
Agree; the code of corporate governance requires it
The COO role varies; it may be a succession role, but many COOs are execution partners, so the board should assess successors on their merits
bank.explanation: The COO role is shaped differently in each company. Some COOs are successors-in-training, others are permanent execution partners. Succession requires the board to assess candidates on merit; no rule requires or forbids a COO becoming CEO.

bank.question: A CIO asks ExCo to approve a USD 15 million core-system upgrade. The CMO says it is 'an IT matter' and does not engage. What is the main risk of this attitude?
options: None; technology investments should be left to the CIO
The system may be designed around technology choices rather than customer and growth needs, and business ownership of the benefits is lost
The CMO may lose budget to the CIO
The board may not be informed of the project
bank.explanation: Technology now shapes customer experience and growth, so the CMO's input is essential and the business must own the benefits. Treating it as 'IT only' is a classic cause of failed tech investments. The budget and board points miss the core issue.

bank.question: In an ExCo debate, a newly hired CIO hesitates and then says she is 'comfortable' with a launch date, though she privately thinks it is unrealistic. Which CEO behaviour would most increase the chance she speaks up next time?
options: Thanking people when they raise risks, sharing his own doubts and inviting challenge before giving his view
Reminding executives that they are paid to speak up
Asking HR to run assertiveness training for the CIO
Moving risk discussions to private one-to-ones with the CEO
bank.explanation: Psychological safety grows when leaders model vulnerability, reward people for raising problems and hold back their own view. Reminders and training put the burden on her, and private one-to-ones take the debate out of the team.

bank.question: A CEO and CFO at a listed cement company often argue in private about growth versus balance-sheet risk, but they always present a single agreed set of numbers to the board. How should the board view this relationship?
options: As a warning sign that the CFO is not supportive of the CEO
As a reason to replace one of them
As healthy constructive tension, provided debates stay on the merits and the CFO keeps her independence on reporting
As a sign that the board should take over capital allocation
bank.explanation: Healthy CEO–CFO tension, with one agreed version of the numbers for the board, is exactly what good governance needs. It becomes a problem only if the CFO's independence on reporting is compromised or if one always overrides the other.

bank.question: Tessaly's board asks for 'a precise forecast' of juice-market growth over ten years to decide on a plant. The strategy team notes that currency swings, consumer spending and sugar taxes could all move sharply. What is the most useful response?
options: Provide a single forecast with a confidence interval of plus or minus 1%
Decline to provide any view because the future is uncertain
Use the most optimistic analyst forecast available, to be ambitious
Explain that this is uncertainty rather than measurable risk, and test the options against a small set of plausible scenarios with signposts
bank.explanation: Where outcomes and odds cannot be reliably known, a precise forecast gives false comfort. Scenarios test which option is robust across futures, and signposts track which one is unfolding. Refusing to give a view or picking the rosiest forecast does not help the board decide.

bank.question: A bank's ExCo spends three meetings debating whether to change the colour scheme of its mobile app, while a decision to sign a ten-year exclusive core-banking contract is approved in twenty minutes. What principle is being violated?
options: Every decision should go to the board
Process should match the decision: move fast on reversible ones and deliberate on high-stakes, hard-to-reverse ones
Technology decisions should be delegated to the CIO
Decisions should be made by majority vote
bank.explanation: The app colour is a cheap two-way door that should be delegated, while the ten-year contract is a one-way door that deserves deep deliberation. The ExCo has the effort upside down. Sending all to the board or delegating all technology decisions is not the principle.

bank.question: A scenario team for a Jakarta hospital chain lists these forces: (1) population growth in Jakarta, which is steady and well understood; (2) whether health insurance becomes widespread, which would transform demand but is highly uncertain; (3) regulatory pricing caps, also high-impact and uncertain; (4) the cost of printer paper. Which pair should form the scenario axes?
options: (2) insurance spread and (3) pricing caps
(1) population growth and (2) insurance spread
(1) population growth and (3) pricing caps
(3) pricing caps and (4) paper costs
bank.explanation: Axes should be critical uncertainties: high impact and high uncertainty, which are (2) and (3). Population growth is predictable, so it belongs in every scenario rather than on an axis, and paper costs have little impact.

bank.question: A port operator in Mombasa weighs a terminal expansion. Option A: build fully now, NPV of +USD 200m (30%), +USD 60m (40%) or −USD 160m (30%). Option B: build a first phase with the right to expand, NPV of +USD 140m (30%), +USD 50m (40%) or −USD 20m (30%). Which statement is correct?
options: Option A has the higher expected value and the same worst case
Both options have the same expected value, so the choice is a matter of taste
Option B has the higher expected value, USD 56m against USD 36m, and a much smaller worst case
Option A has the higher expected value, USD 84m against USD 62m
bank.explanation: Option A: (0.3 × 200) + (0.4 × 60) + (0.3 × −160) = 60 + 24 − 48 = USD 36m. Option B: (0.3 × 140) + (0.4 × 50) + (0.3 × −20) = 42 + 20 − 6 = USD 56m. B wins on expected value and limits the worst case to −USD 20m instead of −USD 160m. The USD 84m and 62m figures ignore the downside scenarios.

bank.question: A seller opens negotiations by stating that their logistics business is 'worth at least USD 300 million'. Your team's later valuations cluster around USD 275–300 million, although your first internal estimate, made months ago, was USD 200 million. Which bias is most likely, and what should the CEO have done?
options: Sunk cost; the team should have ignored the money already spent on due diligence when valuing the business
Groupthink; the CEO should have hired a new valuation team
Overconfidence; the team should have raised its estimate further
Anchoring; the team should have set and documented its own valuation before hearing the seller's number
bank.explanation: The seller's first number has pulled the team's estimates up: classic anchoring. The defence is to fix and document your own valuation range before hearing theirs. Sunk cost relates to past spending, and nothing suggests groupthink or a need to raise estimates.

bank.question: A CEO wants a pre-mortem on a major acquisition but runs it by asking, 'Does anyone see any problems?' at the end of a celebratory presentation. Two people mumble minor concerns. What is the main flaw?
options: The pre-mortem should have been run after the deal closed
It skips the key device: asking people to assume the deal has already failed and write their reasons independently before discussion
Pre-mortems should only include the deal team
The CEO should have asked for problems by email instead
bank.explanation: A pre-mortem works because imagining failure as a fact, and writing reasons independently, makes doubts safe to voice. An open question at the end of a celebration invites polite silence. After closing it would be a post-mortem, and limiting it to the deal team narrows the view.

bank.question: An FMCG company is entering e-commerce in Nigeria for the first time. Nobody knows which platforms, price points or delivery models consumers will adopt. The board demands a fully specified five-year plan before any spending. What is the best advice?
options: Provide the five-year plan, using expert estimates for every assumption
Delay entry until another company proves the model
Treat it as a complex problem: run small, bounded experiments across a few models, learn quickly and scale what works, with clear stop rules
Commit the full five-year budget now to secure first-mover advantage
bank.explanation: Where cause and effect only become clear afterwards, the right approach is probe, sense, respond: small safe-to-fail experiments with stop rules. A detailed plan treats it as merely complicated, and committing the full budget is an unnecessary one-way door.

bank.question: A cement company's board approved a staged expansion with this trigger: 'Proceed to phase two if regional dispatches grow for two straight quarters and coal costs stay within the agreed band.' Two quarters later dispatches are growing but coal costs have broken above the band. What should management recommend?
options: Do not trigger phase two yet; report the signpost status to the board and keep monitoring or revisit the plan
Trigger phase two because demand, the most important signpost, is clearly positive and competitors may move first
Cancel the project permanently
Trigger phase two but delay telling the board until coal costs fall
bank.explanation: The pre-agreed trigger has not been met, so management should not proceed but should report the signposts and revisit with the board. Overriding a pre-agreed signpost because one indicator looks good defeats the discipline, and permanent cancellation overreacts.

bank.question: The CEO of a textile exporter tells ExCo: 'I'm sure this Vietnam joint venture is right. Let's hear your thoughts.' Everyone agrees. Later, three executives admit they had serious doubts. Which pair of changes would best have prevented this?
options: Holding the meeting off-site and allowing more time
Collecting independent written views before discussion, and the CEO sharing his view last
Asking the CFO to prepare a longer and more detailed financial appendix on the joint venture's returns
Inviting the joint-venture partner to present
bank.explanation: Opening with the CEO's conviction anchored the team and triggered deference and groupthink. Independent written views and the CEO speaking last protect against both. Venue, longer appendices or the partner's pitch do nothing to surface suppressed doubts.

bank.question: Two years ago, Tessaly's board approved a well-researched decision to build a powdered-milk plant. A sudden change in import duties has since made imported powder cheaper and the plant is unprofitable. At the review, what is the most useful question to ask first?
options: Who proposed the plant, so accountability is clear?
Should we sell the plant immediately to stop the losses?
Why did management fail to predict the duty change?
Given what was knowable at the time, was the decision process sound, and what does the outcome teach us for the future?
bank.explanation: Separating decision quality from outcome avoids 'resulting'. The board should first judge whether the process was sound given what was knowable, then learn from what happened. Blame, immediate sale or expecting perfect prediction of policy shocks all draw the wrong lessons.

bank.question: A sponsor-family chairman of a listed company starts attending weekly sales meetings and approving individual discounts for key distributors. The CEO feels undermined. What is the best way for the CEO to address it?
options: Accept it, since the family controls the company
Raise it privately with the chairman, framing the line between governing and managing, and agree how the chairman can get the oversight he wants through the board
Complain to the other directors without telling the chairman
Ask the sales team to ignore the chairman's approvals
bank.explanation: The chairman has crossed from governing into managing. The CEO should address it directly and constructively with him, offering board-level ways to give him the oversight he wants. Accepting it, lobbying behind his back or instructing staff to ignore him all damage governance and trust.

bank.question: A company listed in a market whose rules require at least one woman director, as India's and Pakistan's do, proposes a board of seven: the CEO, one other executive, two directors from the founding family and three independent directors, all of them men. Which issue is the clearest gap?
options: There are too many independent directors
The CEO should not sit on the board
There is no female director on the board
Founding-family directors are not allowed
bank.explanation: Where the rules require at least one woman director, as in India and Pakistan, this board does not comply. Three independents out of seven and two executives out of seven are not in themselves the problem, the CEO may sit on the board, and founding-family directors are allowed. Always check exact numbers against the current rules where the company is listed.

bank.question: A CEO wants to remove the head of internal audit after a report criticised a project the CEO sponsored. What makes this especially problematic under widely used governance and internal audit standards?
options: Internal audit reports to the audit committee, and the board's role in removing its head protects audit independence
Heads of internal audit cannot be removed once appointed
Only shareholders can remove the head of internal audit
The external auditor must approve any change
bank.explanation: The head of internal audit reports functionally to the audit committee, and the board or committee is involved in appointing and removing the role precisely to protect independence. Removing the auditor who criticised the CEO's project would undermine that. The other options misstate the standards.

bank.question: A sponsor director proposes that the company rent a new warehouse from his own property firm at a rent he says is 'market'. The board is keen to move fast. Which sequence best protects the company and its minority shareholders?
options: Approve it at the board, then ask the director to declare his interest at the next meeting
Let the CEO approve it within his delegated limits to avoid embarrassing the director
Ask the director to transfer the property to a relative first, so it no longer counts
Have the director declare his interest, benchmark the rent independently, get the audit committee's review, and let the board decide without him, with proper disclosure
bank.explanation: Related-party transactions need prior declaration, arm's-length evidence, audit committee review and a board decision without the interested director, followed by disclosure. Retrospective declaration, routing it under delegated limits or disguising the relationship all defeat the purpose.

bank.question: A company's distributors can be given credit extensions without finance approval, regional bonuses depend entirely on quarterly sales, and managers often say 'everyone pushes stock at quarter end'. As CEO, which action reduces fraud risk across all three sides of the fraud triangle?
options: Add finance approval for credit extensions, rebalance bonuses towards sell-out and quality of revenue, and openly challenge the 'everyone does it' story
Run fraud-awareness training for regional sales teams
Increase the external audit fee to expand testing
Dismiss the regional head with the weakest numbers
